text: Change to passive voice: "Columbus discovered America."
solution: Object "America" becomes the new subject.
The verb "discovered" (simple past) becomes "was discovered" (was + past participle).
The original subject "Columbus" moves after "by".

text: Change to passive voice: "He teaches us English."
solution: This verb has two objects: "us" and "English". Promoting the person, "us", to subject is the more natural passive.
"Teaches" (simple present) becomes "are taught" (are + past participle), matching the new plural subject "we".

text: Change to passive voice: "The teacher checks the homework."
answer: "The homework is checked by the teacher."
solution: Object "the homework" becomes the new subject.
The verb "checks" (simple present) becomes "is checked" (is + past participle).
The original subject "the teacher" moves after "by".

text: Change to passive voice: "The workers are building a new bridge."
answer: "A new bridge is being built by the workers."
solution: Object "a new bridge" becomes the new subject.
The verb "are building" (present continuous) becomes "is being built" (be + being + past participle) — "is" because the new subject, "a new bridge", is singular.
The original subject "the workers" moves after "by".

text: Change to passive voice: "You must submit the report by Friday."
answer: "The report must be submitted by Friday."
solution: Object "the report" becomes the new subject.
The modal "must" stays, and the main verb becomes "be submitted" (be + past participle) right after it.
The agent ("by you") is usually dropped here since it’s already understood from context.

text: Change to passive voice: "They elected him president."
solution: Object "him" becomes the new subject; "president" (the object complement) stays in place after the verb.
The verb "elected" (simple past) becomes "was elected" (was + past participle).

text: Which part of the Tripitaka contains the rules of discipline for Buddhist monks and nuns? (A) Sutta Pitaka  (B) Abhidhamma Pitaka  (C) Jataka tales  (D) Vinaya Pitaka
answer: (D) Vinaya Pitaka. The Vinaya Pitaka lays down monastic rules. The Sutta Pitaka contains the Buddha's sermons and the Abhidhamma Pitaka deals with philosophy; the Jatakas are stories of the Buddha's previous births.

text: In the Battle of Talikota (Rakshasa-Tangadi) of 1565, the Vijayanagara army under Rama Raya was defeated by whom? (A) A confederacy of Deccan Sultanates  (B) The Mughal army of Akbar  (C) The Portuguese of Goa  (D) The Gajapatis of Odisha
answer: (A) A confederacy of Deccan Sultanates. The combined forces of Ahmednagar, Bijapur, Golconda and Bidar, successor states of the Bahmani kingdom, defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota and sacked the capital Hampi.

text: What does the Rummindei (Lumbini) pillar inscription of Ashoka record? (A) Tax concession to Lumbini village  (B) Remorse after the Kalinga war  (C) Ban on killing animals in the capital  (D) Appointment of Dhamma Mahamatras
answer: (A) Tax concession to Lumbini village. The Rummindei inscription records Ashoka's visit to the Buddha's birthplace, exempting the village from bali and reducing bhaga to one-eighth. The Kalinga remorse is in Rock Edict XIII.

text: The Great Bath, a large brick-lined public tank, was discovered at which Harappan site? (A) Harappa  (B) Mohenjo-daro  (C) Lothal  (D) Kalibangan
answer: (B) Mohenjo-daro. The Great Bath is the most famous structure of Mohenjo-daro in Sindh. Mohenjo-daro also yielded the Pashupati seal and the bronze Dancing Girl.

text: The practices of dagh (branding of horses) and chehra (descriptive roll of soldiers) were first introduced in the Sultanate army by which ruler? (A) Alauddin Khalji  (B) Balban  (C) Firoz Tughlaq  (D) Sher Shah
answer: (A) Alauddin Khalji. Alauddin Khalji introduced dagh and chehra to stop fraud in the army and paid soldiers in cash. Sher Shah Suri later revived the same practices, which is why he is a common distractor.

text: The Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple at Thanjavur, a UNESCO World Heritage site, was built by which Chola king? (A) Rajendra I  (B) Parantaka I  (C) Rajaraja I  (D) Vijayalaya
answer: (C) Rajaraja I. Rajaraja I completed the Brihadeshwara temple dedicated to Shiva around 1010 AD. Rajendra I built a similar temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram; Vijayalaya founded the imperial Chola line at Thanjavur.

text: In the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur defeated which ruler to lay the foundation of Mughal rule in India? (A) Rana Sanga  (B) Hemu  (C) Sikandar Lodi  (D) Ibrahim Lodi
answer: (D) Ibrahim Lodi. Babur defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat using artillery and the tulughma tactic. He defeated Rana Sanga the next year at Khanwa.

text: Which Gupta ruler repelled the Huna invasion, an achievement recorded in the Bhitari pillar inscription? (A) Samudragupta  (B) Kumaragupta I  (C) Budhagupta  (D) Skandagupta
answer: (D) Skandagupta. Skandagupta defeated the Hunas around 455 AD; the Bhitari pillar inscription in Uttar Pradesh records this. The pressure of repeated Huna attacks contributed to the later decline of the Guptas.

text: Which Veda is regarded as the origin of Indian music because its hymns were meant to be sung? (A) Yajurveda  (B) Samaveda  (C) Atharvaveda  (D) Rigveda
answer: (B) Samaveda. The Samaveda is the Veda of melodies (saman). The Yajurveda contains sacrificial formulae and the Atharvaveda deals with charms, spells and medicine.

text: The Pali text Milinda Panho records a dialogue between the monk Nagasena and which Indo-Greek king? (A) Demetrius  (B) Antialcidas  (C) Menander  (D) Eucratides
answer: (C) Menander. Menander (Milinda), who ruled from Sakala (Sialkot), questioned Nagasena on Buddhism and is said to have become a Buddhist. Antialcidas sent Heliodorus to the Shunga court.

text: Find the average of 198, 203, 207, 196, and 201 using the deviation method.
solution: Pick base = 200. Deviations from 200: −2, +3, +7, −4, +1.
Sum of deviations = −2 + 3 + 7 − 4 + 1 = 5. Average deviation = 5 / 5 = 1.
Average = base + average deviation = 200 + 1 = 201.
Check by direct addition: 198+203+207+196+201 = 1,005; 1,005/5 = 201. Matches.

text: The average weight of 30 students in a class is 42 kg. When the teacher’s weight is included, the average rises by 1 kg. Find the teacher’s weight.

New average (31 people) = 42 + 1 = 43 kg, so new sum = 31 × 43 = 1,333 kg
Teacher’s weight = new sum − old sum = 1,333 − 1,260 = 73 kg

Girls’ total marks = 2,400 − 1,000 = 1,400, so girls’ average = 1,400 / 20 = 70

text: A boat’s downstream speed is 18 km/hr and its upstream speed is 12 km/hr. Find the boat’s speed in still water, the speed of the stream, and the boat’s average speed for a round trip covering the same distance each way.

solution: Boat speed = (downstream + upstream) / 2 = (18 + 12) / 2 = 15 km/hr.
Stream speed = (downstream − upstream) / 2 = (18 − 12) / 2 = 3 km/hr.
Average round-trip speed = 2 × 18 × 12 / (18 + 12) = 432 / 30 = 14.4 km/hr.

Time downstream = Distance / Speed = 15 / 9 = 5/3 hours = 1 hour 40 minutes.

text: Is the year 2100 a leap year?
answer: No, 2100 is not a leap year
solution: 2100 is divisible by 4 (2100 ÷ 4 = 525), but it is a century year, so it must also be divisible by 400.
2100 ÷ 400 = 5.25, not a whole number — so 2100 is NOT a leap year.

text: If 1 January 2024 was a Monday, what day of the week was 1 January 2025?
solution: 2024 is a leap year (366 days), so it contributes 2 odd days.
Shift Monday forward by 2 days: Monday → Tuesday → Wednesday.

text: Today is Wednesday. What day will it be after 15 days?
solution: 15 ÷ 7 leaves a remainder of 1 (15 = 2×7 + 1), so the odd days are 1.
Shift Wednesday forward by 1 day: Wednesday → Thursday.

text: If 1 January 2024 is a Monday, what day of the week is 1 April 2024?
answer: Monday (if you'd mistakenly used 28 days for February, you'd get 90 days and wrongly land on Sunday)
solution: 2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.
Days from 1 January to 1 April = days in January (31) + February (29) + March (31) = 91.
91 ÷ 7 = 13 exactly, remainder 0 — so 1 April falls on the SAME day as 1 January.

text: Was the year 1900 a leap year? Was the year 2000?
answer: 1900 was not a leap year; 2000 was a leap year
solution: 1900 is divisible by 4, but it’s a century year, so it must also be divisible by 400 to qualify — 1900 ÷ 400 is not a whole number, so 1900 was NOT a leap year.
2000 is also a century year, and 2000 ÷ 400 = 5 exactly, so 2000 WAS a leap year.

text: If 1 January 2020 was a Wednesday, what day of the week was 1 January 2023?
solution: Add up the odd-day contribution of each year from 2020 up to (but not including) 2023: 2020 is a leap year (2 odd days), 2021 is normal (1), 2022 is normal (1).
Total odd days = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.
Shift Wednesday forward by 4 days: Wed → Thu → Fri → Sat → Sun.

text: 36 men can complete a piece of work in 18 days. In how many days will 27 men complete the same work?
solution: More men → fewer days (inverse proportion): days = 36 × 18 / 27.

text: The cost of 8 pens equals the cost of 6 pencils. If the cost of 10 pencils is ₹150, find the cost of 20 pens.
solution: Cost of 1 pencil = 150 / 10 = ₹15, so the cost of 6 pencils = 6 × 15 = ₹90.
The cost of 8 pens equals this: 8 pens = ₹90, so 1 pen = 90/8 = ₹11.25.

text: If 6 men can earn ₹9,000 in 5 days, how much will 8 men earn in 10 days, at the same daily wage rate per man?
solution: Earnings scale up directly with both the number of men and the number of days.

text: If 15 workers can build a wall in 12 days working 8 hours a day, how many days will 18 workers take to build the same wall working 10 hours a day?
solution: More workers → fewer days (inverse): multiply by 15/18.
More hours per day → fewer days (inverse): multiply by 8/10.

text: A garrison of 500 men has food that will last 30 days. After 10 days, 100 more men join. For how many more days will the remaining food last?
solution: Total food stock = 500 × 30 = 15,000 "man-days".
Used in the first 10 days = 500 × 10 = 5,000 man-days. Remaining = 15,000 − 5,000 = 10,000 man-days.
New headcount = 500 + 100 = 600. Remaining days = 10,000 / 600 ≈ 16.67 days.

text: A car covers a certain distance in 5 hours at a speed of 60 km/hr. If the speed is increased to 75 km/hr, find the time taken to cover the same distance.
solution: The distance stays fixed, and speed and time are inversely proportional: time = (5 × 60) / 75.

text: If 20 men can build a 50 m long wall in 12 days, how many days will 15 men take to build a 75 m long wall (at the same rate of work)?
solution: Chain the ratios: fewer men → more days (inverse, multiply by 20/15); more wall to build → more days (direct, multiply by 75/50).

text: Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between growth and development? text: In how many ways can 4 people be seated around a circular table if two particular people must always sit together?
solution: Glue the two people into one block: this leaves 3 entities (the block + 2 other people) to arrange circularly.

The glued pair can sit in 2 internal orders (either person on the left), so total = 2 × 2 = 4.

text: In how many ways can 5 people be seated around a circular table?

text: In how many ways can 7 people be seated around a circular table if two particular people must never sit together?

Arrangements with the two together: glue them into a block (6 entities), circular arrangements = (6−1)! = 120, × 2 internal orders = 240.
Never together = total − together = 720 − 240 = 480.

Find the angle between the hour and minute hands at 3:00.
solution: Hour-hand angle = 30 × 3 + 0.5 × 0 = 90°. Minute-hand angle = 6 × 0 = 0°.
Difference = |90 − 0| = 90°.

text: At what time between 4 and 5 o'clock will the hour and minute hands coincide (overlap exactly)?
solution: Hour-hand angle at M minutes past 4 = 120 + 0.5M. Minute-hand angle = 6M.
For the hands to coincide, set them equal: 6M = 120 + 0.5M → 5.5M = 120 → M = 120/5.5 = 240/11 = 21 9/11.

text: At what time between 9 and 10 o’clock will the hour and minute hands be exactly opposite each other (180° apart)?
solution: Hour-hand angle at M minutes past 9 = 270 + 0.5M. Minute-hand angle = 6M.

For the hands to be opposite, the hour hand (still ahead at this point in the hour) must lead the minute hand by 180°: (270 + 0.5M) − 6M = 180 → 270 − 5.5M = 180 → 5.5M = 90 → M = 90/5.5 = 180/11 ≈ 16.36.
So the hands are opposite at 9 hours and 180/11 minutes, i.e., 16 4/11 minutes past 9.

text: Find the angle between the hour and minute hands at 4:30.
solution: Hour-hand angle = 30 × 4 + 0.5 × 30 = 120 + 15 = 135°. Minute-hand angle = 6 × 30 = 180°.
Difference = |135 − 180| = 45°.

text: The reflection of a clock in a mirror shows the time as 4:20. What is the actual time?
solution: Actual time = 11:60 − mirror time.

text: Find the angle between the hour and minute hands at 7:20.
solution: Hour-hand angle = 30 × 7 + 0.5 × 20 = 210 + 10 = 220°. Minute-hand angle = 6 × 20 = 120°.

text: At what time between 3 and 4 o'clock, after 3:00 itself, will the hands next be at right angles (90° apart)?
solution: At 3:00 exactly, the hands are already 90° apart (hour ahead). As the minute hand gains on the hour hand, this gap shrinks to 0 (coincide) and then grows again with the minute hand now ahead.
The NEXT right angle happens when the minute hand is 90° ahead of the hour hand: 6M − (90 + 0.5M) = 90 → 5.5M = 180 → M = 180/5.5 = 360/11 = 32 8/11.

text: In a certain code language, "pen is good" is written as "ab cd ef", and "good is costly" is written as "ef cd gh". What is the code for "costly" in this language?
solution: "pen", "is", "good" code to "ab", "cd", "ef" (in order) in the first sentence; "good", "is", "costly" code to "ef", "cd", "gh" (in order) in the second.
"is" and "good" are the words common to both sentences, and "cd" and "ef" are the codes common to both coded sentences — so together, {is, good} = {cd, ef}.
"costly" is the only word in the second sentence that does not appear in the first, so its code must be the only code in the second sentence that does not appear among the first sentence’s codes.
That code is "gh".

text: In a code, each letter of a word is replaced by the letter that is the same distance from the end of the alphabet as the original letter is from the start (A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X, and so on). How will FLOWER be coded?
solution: Position from the start: F=6, L=12, O=15, W=23, E=5, R=18.
Mirror position from the end: position p maps to (27 − p) — so F(6)→21=U, L(12)→15=O, O(15)→12=L, W(23)→4=D, E(5)→22=V, R(18)→9=I.
Putting the coded letters together in order: U, O, L, D, V, I.

Apply the same pattern to DOG: D (1st, +1) = E. O (2nd, +2) = Q. G (3rd, +3) = J.

Apply the same rule to DOG: reversed is GOD. Shift each by +1: G→H, O→P, D→E.

Find the amount on ₹10,000 for 6 months at 8% per annum, compounded quarterly.
solution: Quarterly: rate per period = 8/4 = 2%. 6 months = 1/2 year, so number of periods = (1/2) × 4 = 2.

text: ₹10,000 is invested for 1 year at 20% per annum. Compare the compound interest earned if it is compounded annually versus half-yearly.
solution: Half-yearly: 2 periods at 10% each. Amount = 10,000 × (1.10)² = 10,000 × 1.21 = ₹12,100, so CI = ₹2,100.
Half-yearly compounding earns ₹100 more, even with the same 20% annual rate — because the first half-year's interest starts earning its own interest in the second half.

text: A sum, invested at 10% per annum compounded half-yearly, amounts to ₹9,261 after 1.5 years. Find the sum.
solution: Half-yearly: rate per period = 5%, number of periods = 1.5 × 2 = 3. Amount factor = (1.05)³ = 1.157625.
Principal = Amount / factor = 9,261 / 1.157625 = ₹8,000.

text: A sum of ₹20,000, compounded quarterly for 6 months, amounts to ₹20,808. Find the annual rate of interest.
solution: Number of periods = (1/2) × 4 = 2. Amount factor = 20,808 / 20,000 = 1.0404.
1.0404 = (1.02)², so the rate per period = 2%.
Annual rate = 2% × 4 = 8%.

text: Find the compound interest on ₹20,000 for 1 year at 20% per annum, compounded half-yearly.
solution: Half-yearly: rate per period = 20/2 = 10%, number of periods = 1 × 2 = 2.
Compound Interest = 24,200 − 20,000 = ₹4,200.

text: Choose the correct form: If she had saved money earlier, she ___ financially secure today. (A) would be (B) would have been
solution: The cause ("saved money earlier") is in the past, but the result ("today") is in the present — this mixed conditional takes "would be," not "would have been."

text: Choose the correct form: If I ___ a bird, I would fly around the world. (A) am (B) was (C) were (D) will be
solution: This is a present hypothetical that isn’t true (second conditional) — formal English uses "were" for every subject in this pattern, not "was."

text: Choose the correct form: If she had left earlier, she ___ the train. (A) would catch (B) would have caught (C) caught (D) catches
solution: This describes an unreal past situation that didn’t happen — the third conditional, which takes "would have + past participle."

text: Choose the correct form: If water freezes, it ___ into ice. (A) turns (B) will turn (C) would turn (D) would have turned
solution: This describes a general, always-true fact — the zero conditional, which takes present simple in both clauses.

text: Choose the correct form: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ the match. (A) postpone (B) will postpone (C) would postpone (D) would have postponed
solution: This describes a real, possible future situation — the first conditional, which takes "will" in the main clause.

text: Choose the correct form: If he ___ harder in college, he would have a better job now. (A) worked (B) had worked
solution: The result clause is present ("now"), but the "if" clause still describes a past cause, so it still needs the past perfect, "had worked."

solution: "Either...or" needs parallel structure on both sides — "lazy" and "foolish" are both adjectives in (B), while (A) breaks parallelism by switching to a full clause after "or."

Statement: "The number of road accidents at a particular junction has increased significantly over the past year." Courses of Action: I. The traffic police should install proper signals and signage at the junction. II. All vehicles should be banned from using that road permanently.
answer: Only course of action I follows
solution: I: A direct, proportionate step to reduce accidents at that specific junction. This follows.
II: Banning all vehicles permanently is an extreme overreaction not justified by an accident-rate problem. This does not follow.

text: Statement: "Many commuters have complained about overcrowding on a particular bus route during peak hours." Courses of Action: I. The transport authority should increase the frequency of buses on that route during peak hours. II. The transport authority should permanently discontinue that bus route.
answer: Only course of action I follows
solution: I: A direct, proportionate step that targets exactly the described problem (overcrowding at peak hours). This follows.
II: Discontinuing the route removes commuters’ only option and worsens crowding on alternatives — the opposite of a reasonable response. This does not follow.

text: Statement: "Many students in the school have been falling sick due to contaminated water from the school’s old water tank." Courses of Action: I. The school should get the water tank cleaned and the water tested regularly. II. The school should be shut down permanently.
answer: Only course of action I follows
solution: I: Directly and practically addresses the stated cause (the contaminated tank). This follows.
II: Permanently shutting the school is a disproportionate response to a fixable maintenance problem. This does not follow.

text: Statement: "Sales of the company’s flagship product have declined for three consecutive quarters." Courses of Action: I. The company should investigate customer feedback and competitor offerings to understand the decline. II. The company should launch a marketing campaign highlighting the product’s existing strengths.
solution: I: Investigating causes before acting is a sensible first step. This follows.
II: A marketing campaign is also a standard, proportionate business response that can run alongside the investigation. This follows too.

text: Statement: "A particular stationery item’s price has increased slightly due to a rise in raw material costs." Courses of Action: I. The government should impose a complete ban on the sale of that item. II. The company should permanently stop manufacturing all its other products too.
solution: I: A government ban over a slight, cost-driven price increase is wildly disproportionate. This does not follow.
II: Stopping all other products has nothing to do with this one item’s price — a complete non-sequitur. This does not follow.

text: Statement: "A particular medicine has been found to cause mild side effects in a small percentage of patients." Courses of Action: I. The manufacturer should add a clear warning label listing the known side effects. II. The government should ban the medicine completely.
answer: Only course of action I follows
solution: I: A proportionate, standard response to a known but mild and infrequent risk — informs patients without removing a medicine that helps most of them. This follows.
II: A complete ban over mild side effects in only a small percentage of patients is far more drastic than the problem warrants. This does not follow.

text: Statement: "A bridge connecting two villages has developed minor cracks after years of use." Courses of Action: I. The bridge should be permanently closed and never used again. II. The bridge should be inspected by engineers and repaired if needed.
answer: Only course of action II follows

text: Statement: "A school has noticed that many students are arriving late due to traffic congestion near the main gate." Courses of Action: I. The school should consider adjusting the start time slightly to avoid peak traffic hours. II. The school should coordinate with local traffic police to manage congestion near the gate during school hours.

answer: Only course of action I follows

answer: Only course of action I follows

text: A net has A, B, C, D in a horizontal strip, with E above B and F below B. Which face is opposite B?
solution: Keep B as the base. A and C fold up as two opposite side faces.
E and F fold up as the other two side faces.
D is attached beyond C and folds over to close the cube above B.

text: On a standard die, if the face showing 4 is on top, which number is on the bottom face?
solution: The bottom face is opposite the top face: 7 − 4 = 3.

text: A standard die shows 1, 3 and 5 on three visible faces meeting at a corner. What is the sum of the numbers on the three hidden faces?
solution: The six faces of a die always total 1+2+3+4+5+6 = 21.

text: For the same 4 × 4 × 4 painted cube, count all four categories.
answer: 8 with three, 24 with two, 24 with one, 8 with none
solution: Three painted faces: 8 corner cubes.
Exactly two: 12 × 2 = 24. Exactly one: 6 × 2² = 24.
Unpainted: 2³ = 8. Check: 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64.

text: On a standard die, the numbers on opposite faces always add up to 7. If one face shows 2, what number is on the face opposite to it?
On a cube labelled 1 to 6, one view shows 1, 2, 3 and another shows 1, 4, 5 meeting at corners. What is opposite 1?
solution: The first view makes 2 and 3 neighbours of 1. The second makes 4 and 5 neighbours of 1.
All four neighbours are now known. The only remaining label is 6.
No standard-die assumption is needed.

text: Two standard dice are placed together so that the face showing 6 on one die touches the face showing 6 on the other. What is the sum of all the numbers visible on the outside of this combined block?
solution: Two dice together have a total face-sum of 2 × 21 = 42.
The two touching (hidden) faces both show 6, so their sum is 6 + 6 = 12.
Visible sum = 42 − 12 = 30.

text: A cube is painted on all outer faces and cut into 64 equal cubes. How many have exactly two painted faces?
solution: 64 = 4³, so there are four small cubes along each edge.
Exactly two painted faces occur on an edge, excluding its two corner cubes.
There are 12 edges, with 4 − 2 = 2 qualifying cubes each: 12 × 2 = 24.

text: Two standard dice are placed together so that the face showing 3 on one die touches the face showing 4 on the other. What is the sum of all the numbers visible on the outside of this combined block?
An arbitrary cube has 2 next to 1, 3, 5 and 6. What is opposite 2?
answer: 4. It is the remaining label. Using 7 − 2 would incorrectly give 5, which is known to be adjacent.

text: On a standard die, if one face shows 6, what number is on the opposite face?
A cube painted on all sides is cut into 125 equal cubes. How many have exactly one painted face?
answer: 54. Since n = 5, each outer face has (5 − 2)² = 9 non-edge cubes; six faces give 54.

text: A standard die shows 2, 4 and 6 on three visible faces at a corner. Find the sum of the three hidden faces.

answer: 0. All eight cubes are corners with three painted faces; there are no interior edge cubes.

text: For that 5 × 5 × 5 cube, how many small cubes have no paint?
answer: 27. Remove the outer layer: the inner cube is 3 × 3 × 3.

Percentage increase = (10/50) × 100 = 20%.

Profit margin = (Profit / Sales) × 100 = (25 / 75) × 100

March's sales = total − known sum = 310 − 230
= ₹80 thousand

Question: Is x greater than y? Statement I: x = y + 3. Statement II: y is a positive number.
answer: Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not
solution: Statement I alone: x = y + 3 means x exceeds y by exactly 3, for ANY value of y — a definite "yes" regardless of what y actually is — sufficient alone.
Statement II alone: knowing only that y is positive says nothing about x at all — not sufficient.

text: Question: What is the area of a rectangular field? Statement I: The length of the field is 20 metres. Statement II: The perimeter of the field is 60 metres.
solution: Statement I alone: only gives length, not width — can’t find area — not sufficient.
Statement II alone: only gives perimeter, which alone doesn’t pin down a unique length and width combination — not sufficient.
Both together: 2(20 + width) = 60 gives width = 10, so area = 20 × 10 = 200 — a single definite value — sufficient together.

text: Question: Is x an even number? Statement I: x is divisible by 4. Statement II: x is divisible by 6.
solution: Statement I alone: any multiple of 4 is automatically even, so this gives a definite "yes" — sufficient alone.
Statement II alone: any multiple of 6 is also automatically even, so this too gives a definite "yes" — sufficient alone.

text: Question: What is the value of x? Statement I: x + 5 = 12. Statement II: x is a positive integer.
answer: Statement I alone is sufficient, but Statement II alone is not
solution: Statement I alone: x + 5 = 12 gives exactly one value, x = 7 — sufficient alone.
Statement II alone: "a positive integer" allows many values (1, 2, 3, …) — not sufficient alone.

text: Question: What is the value of x? Statement I: x is a prime number less than 10. Statement II: x is an odd number.
answer: Even both statements together are not sufficient
solution: Statement I alone: primes less than 10 are 2, 3, 5, 7 — multiple values, not sufficient.
Statement II alone: infinitely many odd numbers — not sufficient.
Both together: an odd prime less than 10 could be 3, 5, or 7 — still multiple values, not narrowed to one.

text: Question: What is the two-digit number N? Statement I: The sum of the digits of N is 9. Statement II: N is a multiple of 9 and is less than 20.
answer: Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not
solution: Statement I alone: many two-digit numbers have a digit sum of 9 (18, 27, 36, … 90) — not sufficient.
Statement II alone: two-digit multiples of 9 below 20 — only 18 qualifies (9 itself is single-digit, and 27 already exceeds 20) — exactly one value — sufficient alone.

text: Question: What is the value of n? Statement I: n is a multiple of 5. Statement II: n is a two-digit number that is both a multiple of 5 and a perfect square.
answer: Statement II alone is sufficient, but Statement I alone is not (the only two-digit perfect square that’s a multiple of 5 is 25)

text: Choose the correct form: "This novel is ___ than the one I read last month." (A) more interesting (B) most interesting (C) interestinger (D) more interestinger
solution: Comparing exactly two novels needs the comparative degree.
"Interesting" is a longer adjective, so it takes "more" rather than an "-er" suffix — "interestinger" isn’t a real word, and "more interestinger" wrongly combines both forms.

"Tall" is a short, one-syllable adjective, so it takes the "-er" suffix: "taller" — not "more tall".

text: Choose the correct form: "This is the ___ solution to the problem." (A) most perfect (B) more perfect (C) perfect (D) perfectest

text: Choose the correct form: "Of all the players on the team, Arjun played ___." (A) good (B) better (C) best (D) more good

"Good" is irregular — its superlative is "best", not "goodest" or any "-est"/"most" form.

text: Choose the correct form: "Of the two routes, this one is ___." (A) short (B) shorter (C) shortest (D) more shortest

"Short" is a short adjective, so it takes "-er": "shorter".

text: Choose the correct form: "This is ___ building in the city." (A) tall (B) taller (C) tallest (D) the tallest
solution: Comparing this building against ALL other buildings in the city (three or more) needs the superlative degree.
"Tall" takes "-est" for its superlative, and the superlative always takes "the" in front of it: "the tallest".

Change to indirect speech: She said, "I must finish this report today."
answer: She said that she had to finish that report that day.
solution: "Must", expressing a specific one-time obligation, shifts back to "had to".
"This" shifts to "that", and "today" shifts to "that day" since it’s now relative to the moment of speaking, not reporting.

text: Change to indirect speech: She said, "I will finish the work tomorrow."
answer: She said that she would finish the work the next day.
solution: "Will" shifts back to "would" since the reporting verb is past.
"Tomorrow" is relative to the moment of speaking, so it becomes "the next day" in reported speech.
"I" becomes "she" to match the reporting subject.

text: Change to indirect speech: She asked, "Where do you live?"
solution: A wh-question keeps its wh-word ("where") in place of "that"/"if".
The word order reverts to normal statement order ("you live" instead of "do you live"), and the question mark is dropped.

text: Change to indirect speech: He told me, "I can help you with this."
answer: He told me that he could help me with that.
solution: "Can" shifts back to "could" since the reporting verb is past.
"This" shifts to "that" since the speaker’s immediate context is gone in the reported version.
"I" becomes "he", and "you" (the listener, "me" in the original) becomes "me".

text: Change to indirect speech: He asked me, "Do you like coffee?"
answer: He asked me if I liked coffee.
solution: A yes/no question introduces "if" or "whether" in place of "that".
The word order reverts to normal statement order ("you like" instead of "do you like") — the question-style inversion disappears.
"You" refers to the person being asked ("me" in the original), so it becomes "I" in the reported version.

text: Change to indirect speech: He said, "I am tired."
answer: He said that he was tired.
solution: The reporting verb "said" is past, so present simple "am" shifts back to past simple "was".
"I" refers to the person who said it, so it becomes "he" in the reported version.

text: Which greenhouse gas makes the largest contribution to human-caused global warming by total share? (A) Methane  (B) Carbon dioxide  (C) Nitrous oxide  (D) CFCs
answer: (B) Carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels and deforestation accounts for roughly two-thirds of the human-caused greenhouse effect. Methane is more potent per molecule but is emitted in far smaller amounts.

text: The Minamata Convention (2013) on mercury is named after a city in (A) China  (B) South Korea  (C) Japan  (D) Thailand

text: Which biogeochemical cycle has no significant gaseous (atmospheric) phase and is therefore called a sedimentary cycle? (A) Carbon cycle  (B) Nitrogen cycle  (C) Water cycle  (D) Phosphorus cycle

text: One carbon credit is equivalent to the reduction or removal of (A) 1 kg of carbon dioxide  (B) 100 kg of carbon dioxide  (C) 1 tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent  (D) 10 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent

text: Deficiency of which nutrient in the diet causes night blindness? (A) Vitamin A  (B) Vitamin C  (C) Iron  (D) Iodine
answer: (A) Vitamin A. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness; vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, iron deficiency causes anaemia, and iodine deficiency causes goitre.

text: Many class III children believe that heavy objects always sink in water. The MOST effective way for the teacher to address this misconception is to: (A) Tell the children clearly that this belief is wrong and give the correct rule  (B) Ignore it, since the idea will be corrected in higher classes  (C) Ask children to memorise a list of objects that float and sink  (D) Let children test a large wooden log and a small iron nail in water, then discuss what they observe
answer: (D) Let children test a large wooden log and a small iron nail in water, then discuss what they observe. Misconceptions are best dealt with by creating cognitive conflict through hands-on activity and discussion; merely stating the fact does not change children's deeply held ideas.

text: Match the spice with the plant part and choose the correct pair: (A) Cinnamon - leaf  (B) Cardamom - bark  (C) Saffron - root  (D) Turmeric - underground stem
answer: (D) Turmeric - underground stem. Turmeric (haldi), like ginger, is an underground stem (rhizome). Cinnamon is bark, saffron is the stigma of a flower, and cardamom is a fruit with seeds.

text: In the class V chapter 'A Shelter so High!', Gaurav Jani travels by motorcycle from Mumbai to Ladakh and stays with the Changpa people, who live in tents called: (A) Igloo  (B) Bungalow  (C) Jhuggi  (D) Rebo
answer: (D) Rebo. The Changpa, who rear sheep and goats on the cold Changthang plateau of Ladakh, live in rebo, tents made of yak hair wool that are warm and can be moved with the herds.

text: A child answers that 'plants grow because we water them'. The teacher responds, 'Why do you think so? Do all plants need the same amount of water?' This questioning technique is called: (A) Probing  (B) Closed questioning  (C) Rhetorical questioning  (D) Drilling
answer: (A) Probing. Probing questions follow up a child's response to make the child think deeper, justify and refine the idea; they are a key tool of inquiry-based EVS teaching.

text: During a group activity, a teacher notes in her diary: 'Today Ravi, who usually stays quiet, explained to his group why the ice cube melted faster in the sun.' This is an example of: (A) An anecdotal record  (B) A rubric  (C) A portfolio  (D) A standardised test
answer: (A) An anecdotal record. An anecdotal record is a brief, factual, dated note of a significant incident in a child's behaviour or learning; it captures what tests cannot.

text: At the primary stage, Environmental Studies (EVS) is best described as: (A) A simplified version of physics, chemistry and biology  (B) An integrated area of study drawing on science, social science and environmental education  (C) Another name for geography of the local area  (D) Social studies without history
answer: (B) An integrated area of study drawing on science, social science and environmental education. NCF 2005 treats EVS at the primary level as an integrated curricular area that draws on science, social science and environmental education, because the child experiences the environment as a whole.

text: Which of the following animals is nocturnal, that is, active mainly at night? (A) Crow  (B) Peacock  (C) Sparrow  (D) Owl
answer: (D) Owl. Owls and bats are nocturnal; they rest during the day and hunt at night. Crows, peacocks and sparrows are active during the day.

text: Which statement correctly distinguishes Environmental Studies (EVS) from Environmental Education? (A) Both terms mean exactly the same thing in NCF 2005  (B) EVS deals only with pollution, while environmental education deals with plants and animals  (C) Environmental education is taught in primary classes and EVS only in secondary classes  (D) EVS is an integrated curricular area; environmental education focuses on awareness, attitudes and action for protecting the environment

text: Six friends — A, B, C, D, E and F — live in a 3-floor building (floor 1 at the bottom, floor 3 at the top), with two flats on each floor: Left and Right. A lives on floor 1, in the Left flat. solution: A is on floor 1, Left (given). B does not live on floor 2 or 3, and floor 1’s Left flat is already A’s — so B must take floor 1, Right, the only cell left on floor 1.

C does not live in a Right flat, so C must be in a Left flat — on floor 2 or floor 3 (floor 1 is already full).

text: X-rays were discovered by (A) Wilhelm Roentgen  (B) Henri Becquerel  (C) Marie Curie  (D) Ernest Rutherford
answer: (A) Wilhelm Roentgen. Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. Becquerel discovered radioactivity, and Marie Curie isolated radium and polonium.

text: Sulphuric acid, called the 'king of chemicals', is manufactured by the (A) Contact process  (B) Ostwald process  (C) Haber process  (D) Solvay process
answer: (A) Contact process. The contact process oxidises sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst and absorbs it to give H2SO4. The Solvay process makes washing soda and the Ostwald process makes nitric acid.

text: The SI unit of pressure is (A) Newton  (B) Pascal  (C) Joule  (D) Watt
answer: (B) Pascal. Pressure is force per unit area, so its SI unit is newton per square metre, named the pascal (Pa). Newton is the unit of force, joule of energy and watt of power.

text: Which cell organelle is called the 'suicide bag' of the cell? (A) Ribosome  (B) Mitochondrion  (C) Lysosome  (D) Plastid
answer: (C) Lysosome. Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles and, when the cell is damaged, burst and digest the whole cell. Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell and ribosomes make proteins.

text: Permanent hardness of water is due to the presence of dissolved (A) Chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium  (B) Bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium  (C) Carbon dioxide  (D) Sodium chloride
answer: (A) Chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium. Permanent hardness, caused by chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium, cannot be removed by boiling and needs washing soda or ion exchange. Temporary hardness is due to bicarbonates and is removed by boiling.

text: The fuse wire used in household electric circuits should have (A) Low melting point and high resistance  (B) High melting point and low resistance  (C) High melting point and high resistance  (D) Low melting point and low resistance
answer: (A) Low melting point and high resistance. A fuse must heat up and melt quickly when excess current flows, so it is made of a tin-lead alloy with low melting point and high resistance. It is always connected in series with the live wire.

text: The enzyme present in saliva that begins the digestion of starch is (A) Pepsin  (B) Trypsin  (C) Lipase  (D) Ptyalin
answer: (D) Ptyalin. Ptyalin (salivary amylase) converts starch into maltose in the mouth. Pepsin digests protein in the stomach, trypsin acts in the small intestine, and lipase breaks down fats.

text: Sound travels fastest in which of the following? (A) Air  (B) Vacuum  (C) Water  (D) Steel
answer: (D) Steel. Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium; it travels fastest in solids (about 5000 m/s in steel), slower in water (about 1500 m/s) and slowest in air (about 340 m/s). It cannot travel through vacuum at all.

text: When phenolphthalein indicator is added to a basic (alkaline) solution, the solution turns (A) Colourless  (B) Pink  (C) Red  (D) Yellow
answer: (B) Pink. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base. Litmus is red in acid and blue in base, while methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base.

text: A flagpole stands on top of a 20 m tall tower. From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of the bottom of the flagpole is 30°, and the angle of elevation of the top of the flagpole is 45°. Find the length of the flagpole.
solution: Let the horizontal distance from the point to the tower be d. From the bottom of the flagpole (top of the tower, height 20): tan 30° = 20/d, so d = 20√3.
From the top of the flagpole (height 20 + L, where L is the flagpole's length): tan 45° = (20 + L)/d, and since tan 45° = 1, this gives 20 + L = d = 20√3.

text: From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is 30°. After walking 20 m towards the tower, the angle becomes 60°. Find the height of the tower.
solution: Let height = h, and let the original distance be d. From the first position: tan 30° = h/d, so d = h√3.
From the closer position: tan 60° = h/(d − 20), so d − 20 = h/√3.
Substitute: h√3 − 20 = h/√3. Multiply through by √3: 3h − 20√3 = h, so 2h = 20√3, giving h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m.

text: From the top of a cliff 100 m high, the angle of depression of a boat is 30°. Find the distance of the boat from the base of the cliff.
solution: The angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the boat (alternate angles), so tan(30°) = height / distance.
tan(30°) = 1/√3, so 1/√3 = 100 / distance, giving distance = 100√3 ≈ 173.2 m.

text: A ladder leans against a wall, making an angle of 60° with the ground. If the foot of the ladder is 5 m from the wall, find the length of the ladder.
solution: The ladder is the hypotenuse, and 5 m is the side adjacent to the 60° angle: cos(60°) = adjacent / hypotenuse.
cos(60°) = 1/2, so hypotenuse = 5 / (1/2) = 10 m.

text: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point 50 m away from its base is 45°. Find the height of the tower.
solution: tan(45°) = height / distance, so height = distance × tan(45°).
tan(45°) = 1, so height = 50 × 1 = 50 m.

text: A flagpole stands on top of a 10 m tall tower. The angle of elevation of the flagpole's bottom is 30°, and of its top is 60°, from the same point. Find the flagpole's length.
answer: 20 m. d = 10√3 from the 30° angle; 10 + L = d√3 = 30, so L = 20.

In peer tutoring: (A) The teacher teaches each student individually in turn  (B) Parents teach the lesson again at home  (C) Students compete with each other for ranks  (D) A student helps a classmate learn under the guidance of the teacher
answer: (D) A student helps a classmate learn under the guidance of the teacher. Peer tutoring pairs students so that one supports the learning of another; both tutor and tutee benefit, and it is a practical inclusive strategy in large classes. It is cooperative, not competitive.

text: A child repeats the words or phrases spoken to him instead of answering, insists on the same routine every day and gets very upset by small changes. The repetition of others' words is termed: (A) Stammering  (B) Echolalia  (C) Aphasia  (D) Dyslalia
answer: (B) Echolalia. Echolalia, the echoing of words or phrases heard, is commonly seen in autism spectrum disorder along with insistence on sameness. Stammering is a fluency disorder and aphasia a loss of language ability.

text: Which set of signs should alert a primary teacher to a possible visual problem in a child? (A) Reversing letters and reading very slowly  (B) Blurting out answers and losing belongings  (C) Holding the book very close, squinting, rubbing the eyes and complaining of headaches  (D) Repeating others' words and insisting on routines
answer: (C) Holding the book very close, squinting, rubbing the eyes and complaining of headaches. Holding reading material close, squinting, eye rubbing, watering eyes and headaches are warning signs of visual impairment that call for an eye examination. The other sets point to dyslexia, ADHD and autism respectively.

text: Which Article of the Constitution directs every State to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage to children of linguistic minority groups? (A) Article 29  (B) Article 30  (C) Article 350A  (D) Article 46
answer: (C) Article 350A. Article 350A, inserted by the 7th Amendment, deals with facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage. Article 29 protects minority culture, Article 30 their right to run institutions, and Article 46 promotes SC, ST and weaker sections.

text: A principal says: 'Every child should be educated with peers in the regular class as far as possible, and removed only when the nature of the disability makes it unavoidable.' This reflects the principle of: (A) Homogeneous grouping  (B) Least restrictive environment  (C) Medical model of disability  (D) Ability tracking
answer: (B) Least restrictive environment. The least restrictive environment principle requires that children with disabilities be educated with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate. Homogeneous grouping and tracking separate children by ability.

text: According to the classical WHO distinction, loss of a leg is an ___, the resulting inability to walk is a ___, and the inability to get a job because of it is a ___. (A) impairment; disability; handicap  (B) disability; impairment; handicap  (C) handicap; disability; impairment  (D) impairment; handicap; disability
answer: (A) impairment; disability; handicap. In the WHO ICIDH (1980) framework, impairment is loss of body structure or function, disability is the resulting restriction of activity, and handicap is the social disadvantage that follows. The sequence runs body, activity, society.

text: Which of the following best describes inclusive education? (A) Educating children with disabilities in well-equipped special schools with trained staff  (B) Admitting children with disabilities to regular schools and expecting them to adapt to the existing system  (C) Restructuring the school so that all children, with and without disabilities, learn together with the support they need  (D) Teaching children with disabilities separately in a resource room inside a regular school
answer: (C) Restructuring the school so that all children, with and without disabilities, learn together with the support they need. Inclusive education means the school adapts its curriculum, teaching and environment so that all children learn together. Option B describes integration, where the child is expected to adjust to an unchanged school.

text: According to Renzulli's three-ring conception, giftedness arises from the interaction of: (A) Above-average ability, task commitment and creativity  (B) Intelligence quotient, memory and speed of processing  (C) Reading, writing and arithmetic skills  (D) Attention, emotion and motivation
answer: (A) Above-average ability, task commitment and creativity. Joseph Renzulli described gifted behaviour as the overlap of three clusters: above-average (not necessarily superior) ability, high task commitment and creativity. IQ alone is not sufficient in this model.

text: The Taylor frame is an aid used by students with visual impairment mainly for: (A) Reading story books  (B) Drawing and painting  (C) Physical education  (D) Learning arithmetic
answer: (D) Learning arithmetic. The Taylor frame is a slate with star-shaped holes into which metal types are placed to represent digits and signs, enabling blind learners to set out and solve arithmetic problems. The abacus serves a similar purpose.

text: Which group of conditions is covered under 'specific learning disabilities' in the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016? (A) Blindness and low vision  (B) Autism spectrum disorder and cerebral palsy  (C) Thalassemia and haemophilia  (D) Dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia, dyspraxia and developmental aphasia
answer: (D) Dyslexia, dysgraphia, dyscalculia, dyspraxia and developmental aphasia. text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of a country is best defined as: (A) The market value of all goods produced by its citizens anywhere in the world  (B) The market value of all final goods and services produced within its domestic territory in a year  (C) The total income earned by its citizens working abroad  (D) The value of all intermediate goods used in production during a year

text: Major devaluations of the Indian rupee after Independence took place in which pair of years? (A) 1950 and 1975  (B) 1971 and 1980  (C) 1985 and 2008  (D) 1966 and 1991

text: 'Stagflation' describes a situation of: (A) Falling prices along with high growth  (B) Very rapid rise in prices of over 50% a month  (C) High inflation combined with stagnant output and high unemployment  (D) Zero inflation with full employment
answer: (C) High inflation combined with stagnant output and high unemployment. Stagflation = stagnation + inflation: prices rise while growth stalls and unemployment stays high. A monthly price rise of over 50% is hyperinflation.

text: In which year were 14 major commercial banks nationalised in India? (A) 1955  (B) 1980  (C) 1991  (D) 1969

text: Which of the following is a direct tax? (A) Goods and Services Tax  (B) Corporation tax  (C) Customs duty  (D) Excise duty
answer: (B) Corporation tax. A direct tax is paid by the person on whom it is levied and its burden cannot be shifted, e.g. income tax and corporation tax. GST, customs and excise are indirect taxes whose burden is passed to consumers.

text: Primary deficit is equal to: (A) Fiscal deficit plus interest payments  (B) Revenue deficit minus grants for capital assets  (C) Fiscal deficit minus interest payments  (D) Fiscal deficit minus revenue deficit
answer: (C) Fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit minus interest payments on past borrowings. It indicates how much of the current borrowing is for purposes other than servicing old debt.

text: The First Five-Year Plan (1951-56) of India was based on which growth model? (A) Mahalanobis model  (B) Harrod-Domar model  (C) Gadgil formula  (D) Rao-Manmohan model
answer: (B) Harrod-Domar model. The First Plan followed the Harrod-Domar model and gave priority to agriculture and irrigation. The Mahalanobis model was the basis of the Second Plan.

text: The GDP deflator is calculated as: (A) Real GDP divided by nominal GDP, multiplied by 100  (B) Nominal GDP minus real GDP  (C) CPI divided by WPI, multiplied by 100  (D) Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, multiplied by 100

text: In the statements, '@' means '>', '#' means '=', and '$' means '<'. Statements: A @ B, B # C, C $ D. Conclusions: I. A @ D. II. D @ A. Which of the conclusions follow (stated in plain terms)?
solution: Translating: A > B, B = C, C < D. Combining: A > B = C, and separately C < D — so both A and D are simply "greater than C," with no direct link established between A and D themselves.

Try two valid assignments: (B=C=1, A=5, D=10) satisfies everything and gives D > A. But (B=C=1, A=100, D=2) also satisfies everything and gives A > D. Since both outcomes are possible, neither "A > D" nor "D > A" is guaranteed.

text: Statements: P ≥ Q, Q = R, R > S. Conclusions: I. P > S. II. P ≥ S. Which of the conclusions follow?
solution: Since Q = R, the chain becomes P ≥ R > S. Even in the boundary case where P equals R exactly, R > S still makes P > S strictly — so P > S is forced in every valid case.
Since P > S is proven, the weaker P ≥ S is also always true (> always implies ≥). Both conclusions follow, with I being the exact relationship.

text: Statements: M ≤ N, N < O, O = P. Conclusions: I. M < P. II. M < O. Which of the conclusions follow?
solution: N < O and O = P combine to N < P. Since M ≤ N, even in the boundary case M = N, the strict N < P still forces M < P. So Conclusion I is forced.
Similarly, M ≤ N < O forces M < O by the same logic. Conclusion II is forced too.

Try a valid number assignment: B = 1, C = 10, A = 3, D = 3 satisfies every statement (3 > 1, 10 > 1, 10 > 3) but gives A = D exactly — ruling out both "A > D" and "D > A" as safe conclusions.

text: Statements: A ≥ B, B ≥ C. Conclusions: I. A > C. II. A = C. Which of the conclusions follow?

solution: A ≥ B ≥ C combines to A ≥ C — but this is only guaranteed as a non-strict relationship, since both links could be equalities (A = B = C, giving A = C) or could involve a strict step somewhere (e.g. A=3, B=2, C=1, giving A > C).
Since neither "A > C" nor "A = C" is individually guaranteed, but A ≥ C IS guaranteed (and ≥ means one of those two must hold), the answer is "either I or II follows."

A two-year-old says 'Daddy go' and 'More juice', leaving out function words such as articles and auxiliaries. Such utterances are an example of: (A) Telegraphic speech  (B) Egocentric speech  (C) Babbling  (D) Over-generalisation
answer: (A) Telegraphic speech. Telegraphic speech (around 18 to 24 months) keeps only the content words, like an old telegram, dropping articles, prepositions and auxiliaries. Over-generalisation refers to wrongly extending a rule, such as 'foots'.

text: A child from a tribal community enters Class I speaking only her home language, which differs from the school language. The most appropriate strategy for her teacher is to: (A) Make her repeat school-language sentences until she stops using her home language  (B) Keep her in Class I for another year until she learns the school language  (C) Give her written worksheets in the school language to practise at home  (D) Use her home language as a bridge while gradually introducing the school language
answer: (D) Use her home language as a bridge while gradually introducing the school language. The mismatch between home and school language is a major cause of early failure; using the home language as a bridge builds on what the child knows. Suppressing it or holding her back harms both confidence and learning.

text: Chomsky's theory of universal grammar holds that: (A) All languages must be taught using the same textbook  (B) Grammar should be taught before vocabulary in every language  (C) All human languages share a common underlying set of principles that children are born with  (D) Grammar rules are universal because they are learnt through imitation everywhere
answer: (C) All human languages share a common underlying set of principles that children are born with. Universal grammar is the innate set of principles common to all languages, which lets a child acquire any language. It is a nativist, not a behaviourist, idea.

This lesson illustrates: (A) Teaching the four skills in isolation  (B) The grammar-translation method  (C) Exclusive focus on accuracy  (D) Integration of the four language skills

text: Rohan in Class IV reads a passage aloud fluently with correct pronunciation, but cannot answer simple questions about what he has read. His difficulty lies in: (A) Decoding  (B) Phonemic awareness  (C) Comprehension  (D) Letter recognition
answer: (C) Comprehension. Rohan's decoding (converting print to sound) is fine; his problem is comprehension, the construction of meaning. He needs strategies such as predicting, questioning and summarising, not more phonics.

text: According to Krashen, which of the following best describes language 'acquisition' as distinct from language 'learning'? answer: (B) A subconscious process that happens through meaningful exposure and communication. Krashen's acquisition is subconscious and natural, like a child picking up the mother tongue through meaningful use. Learning is the conscious study of rules, which is the main distractor.

text: A Class I teacher says 'Stand up', 'Touch your nose', 'Jump twice', and children respond by performing the actions without speaking. This technique is called: (A) Total physical response  (B) Suggestopedia  (C) Silent way  (D) Community language learning
answer: (A) Total physical response. Total physical response, developed by James Asher, links language to physical action and allows a silent period before speech. It is well suited to beginners and young learners.

text: In a learner-centred language classroom, the role of the teacher is best described as that of a: (A) Facilitator who creates opportunities for learners to use the language  (B) Transmitter who delivers rules and vocabulary to be memorised  (C) Examiner who continuously corrects every mistake  (D) Sole authority who decides what is correct and incorrect
answer: (A) Facilitator who creates opportunities for learners to use the language. In communicative and constructivist classrooms the teacher facilitates, organises tasks, scaffolds and provides input, rather than lecturing or policing errors. Learners are active participants.

text: A teacher explains the rule for the past tense in the mother tongue, then asks students to translate ten Hindi sentences into English. Which method is the teacher using? (A) Direct method  (B) Communicative approach  (C) Grammar-translation method  (D) Total physical response

text: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 4 and their LCM is 48. Find the HCF and the two numbers.

Using the same key, find the value of: 12 + 4 − 5 × 2 ÷ 1
solution: Substitute: 12 ÷ 4 × 5 + 2 − 1.

Addition and subtraction: 15 + 2 = 17, then 17 − 1 = 16.

solution: Substitute: 20 ÷ 4 × 3 + 6 − 2.
Division and multiplication first: 20 ÷ 4 = 5, then 5 × 3 = 15.

solution: Substitute: 12 ÷ 6 × 4 + 3 − 2.

For teaching number recognition and addition to Class 1 children, the most appropriate approach is: (A) Lecture method with worked examples on the board  (B) Play-way method using games, songs, dice and number cards  (C) Deductive method starting from the properties of addition  (D) Written drill of addition facts for 30 minutes daily
answer: (B) Play-way method using games, songs, dice and number cards. The play-way method suits young children, who learn through play and activity. Games with dice and number cards develop number sense while keeping mathematics enjoyable, as NCF 2005 recommends.

text: A Class 1 child counts on her fingers to find 4 + 3. The most appropriate response of the teacher is to: (A) Forbid finger counting because it is a bad habit  (B) Tell her to memorise addition facts before coming to class  (C) Accept it as a natural strategy and gradually help her move to mental strategies such as counting on from 4  (D) Reduce her marks for not using the correct method
answer: (C) Accept it as a natural strategy and gradually help her move to mental strategies such as counting on from 4. Finger counting is a natural stage in developing number sense. The teacher should accept it and gradually support the child in moving towards more efficient strategies rather than banning it.

text: A teacher plans to teach decimals only after children are comfortable with fractions and place value. This decision is based on which characteristic of mathematics? (A) Its symbolic nature  (B) Its precision  (C) Its aesthetic nature  (D) Its hierarchical (sequential) nature
answer: (D) Its hierarchical (sequential) nature. Mathematics is hierarchical: each concept builds on earlier ones, so decimals (tenths, hundredths) require prior understanding of fractions and place value.

text: A student solves 52 - 27 = 35 and 73 - 48 = 35. The most likely reason for these errors is that the student: (A) Has forgotten the subtraction facts  (B) Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in each column and does not understand regrouping (borrowing)  (C) Is adding instead of subtracting  (D) Does not know how to write two-digit numbers
answer: (B) Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in each column and does not understand regrouping (borrowing). In both cases the child does 7 - 2 and 8 - 3 instead of regrouping a ten. This systematic error shows that the procedure of borrowing is not understood conceptually.

text: A Class 7 student argues, 'Every square is a rectangle because it has all the properties of a rectangle, but a rectangle need not be a square.' This reasoning corresponds to which Van Hiele level? (A) Informal deduction (abstraction)  (B) Visualisation  (C) Rigour  (D) Analysis
answer: (A) Informal deduction (abstraction). Relating classes of shapes by their properties (class inclusion) and giving informal arguments is the informal deduction level. At analysis level a child lists properties but does not see the relation between classes.

text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the nature of mathematics? (A) It is hierarchical: later concepts depend on earlier ones  (B) It uses precise symbols with agreed meanings  (C) Its results are established by repeated empirical observation rather than by proof  (D) It is abstract and deals with ideas rather than physical objects
answer: (C) Its results are established by repeated empirical observation rather than by proof. Mathematics is deductive: results are proved logically from definitions and axioms, not verified by experiment. Being hierarchical, symbolic, precise and abstract are all accepted characteristics.

text: Which teaching-learning material is most suitable for showing that adding a negative integer means moving in the opposite direction, as in 5 + (-3) = 2? (A) Number line  (B) Tangram  (C) Fraction strips  (D) Geoboard
answer: (A) Number line. On a number line, adding a positive number is a move to the right and adding a negative number is a move to the left, which makes integer operations visible. The other materials deal with shapes or fractions.

text: Which statement about the deductive method of teaching mathematics is correct? (A) It starts from particular examples and leads to a general rule  (B) It is the best method for introducing a new concept to young children  (C) It states the rule or formula first and then applies it to examples; it saves time but does not by itself build understanding  (D) It is the same as the heuristic method
answer: (C) It states the rule or formula first and then applies it to examples; it saves time but does not by itself build understanding. The deductive method proceeds from the general rule to particular cases. It is quick and useful for practice and for older students, but it should follow inductive discovery, not replace it, when introducing new concepts.

text: Asked to fill the blank in 8 + 4 = __ + 5, most children in a class write 12. This error reveals that they: (A) Interpret the equals sign as 'the answer comes next' rather than as a symbol of balance or equivalence  (B) Do not know that 8 + 4 is 12  (C) Cannot add three numbers  (D) Have understood the commutative property
answer: (A) Interpret the equals sign as 'the answer comes next' rather than as a symbol of balance or equivalence. Children often see '=' as an instruction to compute, not as 'is the same as'. The correct answer is 7, and a pan balance helps children see both sides as equal quantities.

text: A mathematics laboratory in a school is mainly intended to: (A) Replace the mathematics textbook completely  (B) Prepare students for mathematics olympiads only  (C) Provide a space where students verify and discover mathematical ideas through activities, models and manipulatives  (D) Conduct written examinations in a separate room
answer: (C) Provide a space where students verify and discover mathematical ideas through activities, models and manipulatives. A mathematics laboratory supports learning by doing: students handle manipulatives, make models and perform activities that make abstract concepts concrete. A mathematics club similarly fosters interest through puzzles, projects and exhibitions.

text: A container has 40 litres of pure milk. 8 litres are withdrawn and replaced with water, and this process is repeated once more. Find the quantity of pure milk left after the two operations.
solution: Each operation removes a fraction x/V = 8/40 = 1/5 of whatever is currently in the container.
After n operations, pure liquid left = V × (1 − x/V)ⁿ = 40 × (1 − 1/5)² = 40 × (4/5)²

text: A milkman mixes water (free) with milk and sells the mixture at the same price as pure milk, thereby gaining 20%. Find the ratio of water to milk in the mixture.
solution: Let the price of pure milk (and the selling price of the mixture) = ₹6/litre. A 20% gain means the mixture’s own cost price = SP ÷ 1.2 = 6 ÷ 1.2 = ₹5/litre.
Apply alligation with water (₹0) as the "cheaper" item and milk (₹6) as the "dearer" item, mean = ₹5: water : milk = (6 − 5) : (5 − 0) = 1 : 5.

text: In what ratio should tea worth ₹60/kg be mixed with tea worth ₹80/kg so that the mixture is worth ₹65/kg?
solution: Using the alligation rule: cheaper : dearer = (80 − 65) : (65 − 60) = 15 : 5 = 3 : 1.
Check: weighted average = (3 × 60 + 1 × 80) / 4 = (180 + 80) / 4 = 260/4 = 65 — matches.

Choose the correct modal: You ___ finish this today; there is no urgency, you can do it tomorrow if you prefer. (A) must (B) need not (C) may not (D) should not
solution: The sentence describes an absence of obligation ("no urgency"), not a prohibition — "need not" is correct, not "must not."

text: Choose the correct modal: She has been studying for ten hours straight; she ___ be exhausted by now. (A) can (B) must (C) may (D) should
solution: The sentence draws a confident logical conclusion from the evidence given (ten hours of studying) — "must" expresses this kind of near-certain deduction.

text: Choose the correct modal: ___ I open the window? It’s getting a bit warm in here. (A) Must (B) May (C) Should (D) Need
solution: This is a formal request for permission — "May" is the standard modal for asking permission.

text: Choose the correct modal: Despite the heavy traffic, he ___ reach the station on time. (A) could (B) was able to
solution: This describes one specific accomplished action despite a difficulty (the traffic) — "was able to" is preferred here over the general-ability "could."

text: Choose the correct modal: You ___ park here; it is a no-parking zone, so please move your car. (A) must not (B) need not (C) may (D) should
solution: The sentence describes a prohibition (a no-parking zone) — "must not" is the correct modal for forbidding something.

text: Choose the correct modal: As a child, she ___ run very fast. (A) could (B) was able to
solution: This describes a general ability spread over her childhood, not one single event — "could" is the natural choice.

text: Check whether 9,251 is divisible by 11.
solution: From the right: position 1 = 1, position 2 = 5, position 3 = 2, position 4 = 9.
Sum of odd positions (1st, 3rd) = 1 + 2 = 3. Sum of even positions (2nd, 4th) = 5 + 9 = 14.
Difference = |3 − 14| = 11, which is divisible by 11 — so 9,251 is divisible by 11.

text: Find the number of trailing zeros in 100!.

A invests ₹30,000 at the start of the year. B joins the business after 3 months with ₹45,000. Find the profit-sharing ratio for that year.

text: A invests ₹40,000 and manages the business, while B invests ₹60,000 as a sleeping partner. A receives 10% of the total profit as a management fee, and the rest is split in the ratio of their capitals. If the total profit is ₹25,000, find B’s total share.
solution: Management fee (A only) = 10% of 25,000 = ₹2,500. Remaining profit to split = 25,000 − 2,500 = ₹22,500.
Capital ratio A : B = 40,000 : 60,000 = 2 : 3.
B’s share of the remainder = (3/5) × 22,500 = ₹13,500. (B gets no management fee, so this is B’s total share.)

text: A starts a business with ₹20,000. After 4 months, he adds a further ₹10,000. B joins at the very start with ₹25,000 and keeps it invested for the whole 12-month year. Find the profit-sharing ratio.
solution: A's capital-months in two stretches: ₹20,000 for the first 4 months, then ₹30,000 for the remaining 8 months.

text: A and B invest in a business for the same time period. Their profits come out in the ratio 4 : 5. If A invested ₹8,000, find B's investment.
solution: Since the time period is the same for both, the capital ratio equals the profit ratio: A : B = 4 : 5.

text: A invests ₹10,000 for 12 months and B invests ₹15,000 for 8 months in a business. At the end, they earn a profit of ₹6,200. Find each partner’s share.
solution: The capitals alone (10,000 vs 15,000) are NOT the ratio to use, since the time periods differ — use capital × time instead.
A: 10,000 × 12 = 1,20,000. B: 15,000 × 8 = 1,20,000. The two products are actually equal, so the ratio is 1 : 1, even though the capitals themselves weren’t equal.
Each partner gets half of ₹6,200 = ₹3,100.

text: A and B start a business with capitals of ₹8,000 and ₹12,000 respectively, investing for the same time period. At the end of the year, they earn a profit of ₹5,000. Find each partner’s share.
solution: Since the time period is the same for both, the ratio is simply the capital ratio: 8,000 : 12,000 = 2 : 3.

text: A, B and C invest in a business in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5, for the same time period. If the total profit is ₹20,000, find C’s share.
solution: Sum of ratio terms = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10.

text: The price of rice rises by 25%. By what percentage should consumption fall to keep spending unchanged?
solution: Spending = price × quantity. Let the old price and quantity each be 100.
New price = 125. To keep the product 10,000, new quantity = 10,000/125 = 80.
Quantity falls from 100 to 80, a 20% reduction.

text: A committee of 3 people is to be formed from 5 men and 4 women, with exactly 2 men and 1 woman. In how many ways can this be done?
solution: Choosing 2 men from 5: ⁵C₂ = 10. Choosing 1 woman from 4: ⁴C₁ = 4.
These two choices are independent, so multiply them: 10 × 4 = 40.

text: In how many ways can 3 books be selected from a shelf of 8 different books?
solution: Selecting books (the group chosen, not an order among them) is a combination.

text: In how many ways can a President and a Secretary be chosen from a group of 6 people, assuming one person can’t hold both positions?
solution: The two roles are distinct (President ≠ Secretary), so who gets which role matters — this is a permutation.

text: In how many ways can 5 people be seated in a row such that 2 particular people always sit together?
solution: Glue the 2 particular people into one block. This leaves 4 units to arrange: the block plus the other 3 people.
These 4 units can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways.
Within the block, the 2 people can switch places in 2! = 2 ways.

text: A password consists of 2 letters (A–Z) followed by 3 digits (0–9), with repetition allowed in both parts. How many different passwords are possible?
solution: This is the fundamental counting principle applied step by step, not a selection of a subset.
Letters: 26 choices for each of 2 positions = 26² = 676. Digits: 10 choices for each of 3 positions = 10³ = 1,000.
Total passwords = 676 × 1,000 = 6,76,000.

text: In how many ways can the letters of the word "MANGO" be arranged?
solution: MANGO has 5 distinct letters, and arranging them is a permutation of all 5.
Number of arrangements = 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

text: In how many ways can the letters of the word "BANANA" be arranged?
solution: BANANA has 6 letters in total: B occurs once, A occurs 3 times, N occurs 2 times.

text: A committee of 4 is to be formed from 6 men and 4 women, with at least 2 women. In how many ways can this be done?
solution: Split into cases by the exact number of women: 2, 3, or 4.
Exactly 2 women, 2 men: ⁴C₂ × ⁶C₂ = 6 × 15 = 90.
Exactly 3 women, 1 man: ⁴C₃ × ⁶C₁ = 4 × 6 = 24.
Exactly 4 women, 0 men: ⁴C₄ × ⁶C₀ = 1 × 1 = 1.

In how many ways can 4 people be seated in a row such that 2 particular people always sit together?

solution: Combine the percentages first: Rent + Transport = 30% + 15% = 45%.

text: In a pie chart, four categories take up 80°, 100°, 70° and 60°. Find the degree and the percentage of the fifth (unstated) category.
solution: Sum of the known degrees = 80 + 100 + 70 + 60 = 310°.
Remaining degree = 360° − 310° = 50°.

text: In a pie chart, the angle representing a company’s Marketing budget is 72°. If the total budget is ₹15,00,000, find the amount allocated to Marketing.

text: Using the same company budget (total ₹15,00,000), if R&D is allocated 90° and Operations is allocated 108°, find the combined percentage of R&D and Operations.

Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours, and Pipe B can fill it in 15 hours. Pipe A is opened first, and Pipe B joins 4 hours later. Find the total time taken to fill the tank.
solution: In the first 4 hours, only A works: it fills 4 × (1/12) = 1/3 of the tank. Remaining = 2/3.
Once both are open, combined rate = 1/12 + 1/15 = 5/60 + 4/60 = 9/60 = 3/20.
Time to fill the remaining 2/3 at this rate = (2/3) ÷ (3/20) = (2/3) × (20/3) = 40/9 hours.
Total time = 4 + 40/9 = 36/9 + 40/9 = 76/9 ≈ 8.44 hours (8 hours and about 27 minutes).

text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 6 hours, and Pipe B can fill the same tank in 8 hours. If both pipes are opened together, how long will it take to fill the tank?

Two pipes can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours respectively. A third outlet pipe can empty the full tank in 20 hours. If all three are opened together, how long will it take to fill the empty tank?
solution: Rates: 1/12, 1/15, and −1/20. Using 60 as a common denominator: 5/60 + 4/60 − 3/60 = 6/60 = 1/10.
Time = 1 ÷ (1/10) = 10 hours.

text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 6 hours. When pipe A and an outlet pipe B are opened together, the tank fills in 10 hours. Find the time pipe B alone would take to empty the full tank.
solution: Set up the combined-rate equation with B's rate as the unknown: 1/6 − 1/y = 1/10.
So y = 15 hours.

text: A tank can be filled by Pipe A in 4 hours. Pipe A is twice as fast as Pipe B. If both pipes work together, how long will they take to fill the tank?
solution: Pipe A’s rate = 1/4. "A is twice as fast as B" means A’s rate is double B’s rate, so B’s rate = (1/4) ÷ 2 = 1/8 (B alone would take 8 hours).

text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 5 hours, while Pipe B (an outlet) can empty the full tank in 10 hours. If both pipes are opened together, how long will it take to fill the empty tank?
solution: Time = 1 ÷ (1/10) = 10 hours.

text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 15 and 20 hours respectively. Both are opened together, but after 4 hours, Pipe A is closed. Find the total time taken to fill the tank.
solution: Combined rate for the first 4 hours = 1/15 + 1/20 = 4/60 + 3/60 = 7/60.
Filled in 4 hours = 4 × 7/60 = 28/60 = 7/15. Remaining = 8/15.
Only B works after this, at rate 1/20. Time for the rest = (8/15) ÷ (1/20) = (8/15) × 20 = 160/15 = 32/3 hours ≈ 10.67 hours.
Total time = 4 + 32/3 = 12/3 + 32/3 = 44/3 ≈ 14.67 hours (about 14 hours 40 minutes).

text: Pipe A can fill a tank in 6 hours, while Pipe B (an outlet) can empty the full tank in 9 hours. If both are opened together, how long will it take to fill the empty tank?

Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 and 24 hours respectively. Both are opened together, but after 4 hours, Pipe A is closed. Find the total time to fill the tank.
answer: 16 hours. First 4 hrs (combined rate 1/8) fill 1/2; remaining 1/2 at B's rate 1/24 takes 12 hrs; total 4+12.

text: A tank is filled by Pipe A in 9 hours. Pipe A is 1.5 times as fast as Pipe B. If both work together, how long will they take to fill the tank?

text: Two coins are tossed together. Find the probability of getting at least one head.
solution: Total outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT — 4 in all.
It’s easier to find the opposite first: P(no heads) = P(TT) = 1/4.
P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

text: A die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a number greater than 4.
solution: Numbers greater than 4 on a standard die: 5 and 6 — that’s 2 favorable outcomes out of 6 total.
Probability = 2/6 = 1/3.

text: A bag contains 4 red balls and 6 green balls. Two balls are drawn at random together. Find the probability that both are red.
solution: Drawing 2 balls together is a selection, so count with combinations.
Total ways to choose any 2 from 10: ¹⁰C₂ = 45. Favorable ways to choose 2 red from 4: ⁴C₂ = 6.
Probability = 6/45 = 2/15.

text: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled together. Find the probability of getting a head on the coin AND a number greater than 4 on the die.
solution: These are independent events. P(head) = 1/2. P(number > 4) = 2/6 = 1/3.
P(both) = P(head) × P(number > 4) = (1/2) × (1/3)

text: A bag contains 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is blue.
solution: Total balls = 5 + 3 = 8. Favorable outcomes (blue) = 3.
Probability = 3/8.

text: A card is drawn at random from a standard deck of 52 playing cards. Find the probability that it is either a King or a Queen.
solution: There are 4 Kings and 4 Queens, and a single card can’t be both — these are mutually exclusive.

text: The same bag (4 red, 6 green) is used, but now 2 balls are drawn one after another WITHOUT replacement. Find the probability that both are red, and check it against the previous answer.
solution: P(first red) = 4/10. Given the first was red, 3 red remain out of 9 total, so P(second red) = 3/9.
This matches the combination-based answer from the previous example, as it should — both methods describe the same situation.

text: Two dice are rolled together. Find the probability that the sum of the two numbers is 7.
solution: Total equally likely outcomes = 6 × 6 = 36.
Pairs that sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — 6 favorable outcomes.
Probability = 6/36 = 1/6.
