text: Five years ago, the ratio of A's and B's ages was 3 : 5. Ten years from now, the ratio will be 3 : 4. Find their present ages.
solution: Let present ages be A and B. Five years ago: (A−5)/(B−5) = 3/5 → 5A − 25 = 3B − 15 → 5A − 3B = 10 … (1)
Subtract (2) from (1): A = 20. Substitute into (2): 4(20) − 3B = −10 → 80 − 3B = −10 → B = 30.
Check: 5 years ago, 15 : 25 = 3 : 5. 10 years from now, 30 : 40 = 3 : 4. Both match.

text: A grandfather is 4 times as old as his grandson. In 8 years, the grandfather will be 3 times as old as the grandson will be then. Find their present ages.
solution: Let the grandson's present age = x, so the grandfather's present age = 4x.
Grandson = 16, Grandfather = 64. Check: in 8 years, grandson = 24, grandfather = 72, and 72 = 3 × 24.

text: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 4 : 5. Eight years ago, their ages were in the ratio 3 : 4. Find their present ages.
solution: Let A = 4x and B = 5x.
Eight years ago: A − 8 = 4x − 8, B − 8 = 5x − 8. Given: (4x − 8) / (5x − 8) = 3 / 4.

text: The sum of the present ages of a mother and her daughter is 40 years. Five years ago, the mother’s age was 4 times the daughter’s age. Find their present ages.
solution: Let the daughter’s present age = x, so the mother’s present age = 40 − x.
Five years ago: daughter = x − 5, mother = 35 − x. Given: 35 − x = 4(x − 5) → 35 − x = 4x − 20 → 55 = 5x → x = 11.
Daughter = 11, Mother = 40 − 11 = 29. Check: 5 years ago, daughter = 6, mother = 24, and 24 = 4 × 6.

text: Five years ago, Rohan’s age was three times his daughter’s age. Ten years from now, Rohan’s age will be twice his daughter’s age. Find their present ages.
solution: Let the daughter’s present age = x and Rohan’s present age = y.
Five years ago: y − 5 = 3(x − 5) → y = 3x − 10 … (1)
Ten years from now: y + 10 = 2(x + 10) → y = 2x + 10 … (2)

text: A father is 3 times as old as his son. After 12 years, the father will be twice as old as his son. Find their present ages.
solution: Let the son’s present age = x, so the father’s present age = 3x.
After 12 years: father = 3x + 12, son = x + 12. Given: 3x + 12 = 2(x + 12) → 3x + 12 = 2x + 24 → x = 12.
Son = 12, Father = 36. Check: after 12 years, father = 48, son = 24, and 48 = 2 × 24.

text: The difference between the ages of a father and his son is 24 years. In 4 years, the father will be 4 times as old as the son will be then. Find their present ages.
solution: Let the son's present age = x, so the father's present age = x + 24 (the age difference stays 24 years at every point in time).
Son = 4, Father = 28. Check the difference: 28 − 4 = 24. Check the given condition: in 4 years, father = 32, son = 8, and 32 = 4 × 8.

text: The difference between the ages of two friends is 15 years. Eight years ago, the elder was twice as old as the younger. Find their present ages.
answer: Younger = 23 years, Elder = 38 years. Elder = younger+15; 8 years ago, (younger+15−8) = 2(younger−8).

text: Six years ago, a man was 4 times as old as his son. Six years from now, he will be twice as old as his son. Find their present ages.
The present ages of P and Q are in the ratio 5 : 7. Six years ago, their ages were in the ratio 2 : 3. Find their present ages.
Five years ago, the ratio of X's and Y's ages was 1 : 2. Ten years from now, the ratio will be 2 : 3. Find their present ages.
answer: X = 20 years, Y = 35 years. Set up (X−5)/(Y−5)=1/2 and (X+10)/(Y+10)=2/3, then solve together.

text: The sum of the present ages of a man and his wife is 72 years. Four years ago, the ratio of their ages was 5 : 3. Find their present ages.
answer: Man = 44 years, Wife = 28 years. (M−4)/(W−4)=5/3 with M+W=72.

text: A mother is 5 times as old as her daughter. In 6 years, she will be 3 times as old as the daughter will be then. Find their present ages.
answer: Daughter = 6 years, Mother = 30 years. 5x+6 = 3(x+6) gives x = 6.

A mother is 5 times as old as his daughter now. After 10 years, the mother will be 3 times as old as the daughter. Find mother's present age.
explanation: Let the daughter's present age be s. mother's age = 5s. After 10 years: 5s+10 = 3(s+10) → s = 10. So mother = 50, daughter = 10, sum = 60, difference = 40.

text: Two trains, 120 m and 180 m long, run on parallel tracks in the SAME direction at 72 km/hr and 54 km/hr. Find the time for the faster train to completely cross the slower one.
solution: Same direction, so relative speed = difference of speeds = 72 − 54 = 18 km/hr.
Convert to m/s: 18 × 5/18 = 5 m/s.
Distance to cover = sum of both lengths = 120 + 180 = 300 m.
Time = Distance / Speed = 300 / 5 = 60 seconds.

text: A train 150 m long running at 70 km/hr crosses a man walking in the SAME direction at 10 km/hr. Find the time taken to cross him.
solution: Same direction, so relative speed = 70 − 10 = 60 km/hr.
Convert to m/s: 60 × 5/18 = 50/3 m/s.
Time = Distance / Speed = 150 / (50/3) = 150 × 3/50 = 9 seconds.

text: A train 180 m long is running at 54 km/hr. How long will it take to cross a man standing on the platform?
solution: Convert speed to m/s: 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s.
Crossing a man (a point) means covering a distance equal to the train’s own length: 180 m.
Time = Distance / Speed = 180 / 15 = 12 seconds.

text: Two trains, 140 m and 160 m long, run on parallel tracks in OPPOSITE directions at 60 km/hr and 48 km/hr. Find the time for them to cross each other.
solution: Opposite directions, so relative speed = sum of speeds = 60 + 48 = 108 km/hr.
Convert to m/s: 108 × 5/18 = 30 m/s.
Distance to cover = sum of both lengths = 140 + 160 = 300 m.
Time = Distance / Speed = 300 / 30 = 10 seconds.

text: Two trains start at the same time from stations A and B towards each other. After crossing each other, they take 4 hours and 9 hours respectively to reach stations B and A. Find the ratio of their speeds.
solution: Using the shortcut: speed of train from A / speed of train from B = √(b/a), where a = 4 (A-train's remaining time) and b = 9 (B-train's remaining time).
So the speeds are in the ratio 3 : 2 — the train from A is faster, consistent with it needing less time to finish its remaining distance.

text: A train 200 m long is running at 66 km/hr. It crosses a man walking in the OPPOSITE direction at 6 km/hr. Find the time taken to cross him.
solution: Opposite directions, so relative speed = 66 + 6 = 72 km/hr.
Convert to m/s: 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.
Distance to cover is just the train's length (the man has no length): 200 m. Time = 200 / 20 = 10 seconds.

text: A train 150 m long running at 72 km/hr crosses a platform in 25 seconds. Find the length of the platform.
solution: Convert speed to m/s: 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.
Distance covered in 25 seconds = 20 × 25 = 500 m.
This distance is the train’s length plus the platform’s length, so platform length = 500 − 150 = 350 m.

text: A train crosses a man standing on a platform in 10 seconds, and crosses the entire 300 m long platform in 25 seconds. Find the length and speed of the train.
answer: Length = 200 m, Speed = 20 m/s. Let speed = s; train length = 10s; 10s + 300 = 25s gives s = 20.

A shopkeeper buys a table for ₹1,200 and sells it for ₹1,500. Find his profit percentage.
A trader marks his goods 40% above cost price, then allows a discount of 10% on the marked price. Find his profit percentage.
solution: Let CP = 100. Marked Price = 100 × 1.40 = 140
Profit = 126 − 100 = 26, so Profit% = 26%
Check with the successive-change formula: a=+40, b=−10 → net% = 40 − 10 + (40×−10)/100 = 30 − 4 = 26%.

text: A dishonest dealer claims to sell rice at cost price but uses a weight of 800 g instead of 1 kg. Find his gain percentage.
solution: He charges the cost-price rate for 1,000 g but actually hands over only 800 g, so his real cost is only for 800 g.
Let the price per gram equal his cost per gram, c. Revenue collected = 1,000c (he bills for 1 kg). Actual cost = 800c (what he really gave).
Gain = 1,000c − 800c = 200c. Gain% on his actual cost = (200c / 800c) × 100

text: An article marked at ₹2,000 is sold after a discount of 15%. Find the selling price.
A man sells a watch for ₹1,140 at a loss of 5%. Find the cost price.
A trader marks an item 25% above its cost price but still ends up making a profit of only 12.5% after a discount. Find the discount percentage.
solution: Let CP = 100, so MP = 125 and (since profit is 12.5%) SP = 112.5.
Discount amount = MP − SP = 125 − 112.5 = 12.5

text: Two items are each sold for ₹1,200. On one, a shopkeeper gains 20%; on the other, he loses 20%. Find his overall loss or gain percentage on this pair.
answer: 4% loss (not a break-even, even though the percentages look equal and opposite)
solution: CP of the first item = SP / 1.20 = 1,200 / 1.20 = 1,000.
CP of the second item = SP / 0.80 = 1,200 / 0.80 = 1,500.
Check against the identity: equal gain and loss of x% = 20% on equal selling prices always gives a loss of (x/10)% squared = (20/10)² = 4%. Matches.

Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) She finished her work quickly, she went home early. (B) She finished her work quickly; she went home early.
answer: (B) She finished her work quickly; she went home early.
solution: These are two closely related independent clauses with no connecting word — joining them with only a comma is a comma splice; a semicolon is correct here.

text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) The childrens toys were scattered across the room. (B) The children’s toys were scattered across the room.
answer: (B) The children’s toys were scattered across the room.
solution: "Children" is already plural and does not end in s, so its possessive is formed with apostrophe + s: "children’s".

text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) She packed three things: a map, a torch, and water. (B) She packed three things, a map, a torch, and water.
answer: (A) She packed three things: a map, a torch, and water.
solution: A colon, not a comma, is used after a complete independent clause to introduce the list that follows.

text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) Although it was raining we decided to go for a walk. (B) Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.
answer: (B) Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.
solution: The sentence opens with a subordinate clause ("Although it was raining") before the main clause, which needs a comma after it.

text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) The teacher said, "Submit your assignments by Friday." (B) The teacher said "Submit your assignments by Friday".
answer: (A) The teacher said, "Submit your assignments by Friday."
solution: A comma is needed before a direct quotation, and the closing punctuation belongs inside the quotation marks.

text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) I need to buy apples, bananas, and oranges from the market. (B) I need to buy apples bananas and oranges from the market.
answer: (A) I need to buy apples, bananas, and oranges from the market.
solution: Three or more items in a list need commas separating them.

text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) It started to rain heavily, the match was postponed. (B) It started to rain heavily; the match was postponed.
answer: (B) It started to rain heavily; the match was postponed.

text: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence. (A) Its going to be a long day. (B) It’s going to be a long day.
answer: (B) It’s going to be a long day.

text: I. x² − 8x + 15 = 0  II. y² − 2y − 15 = 0. Find the relationship between x and y.
solution: II: y² − 2y − 15 = (y − 5)(y + 3) = 0, so y = 5 or −3. The negative product of roots (−15) for equation II was a hint that one root would be negative.
Comparing every pair: (3,5)→x<y, (3,−3)→x>y, (5,5)→x=y, (5,−3)→x>y. The results genuinely conflict (both > and < occur), so the relationship cannot be determined.

text: I. x² − 7x + 12 = 0  II. y² − 3y + 2 = 0. Find the relationship between x and y.
solution: Every value of x (3 or 4) is bigger than every value of y (1 or 2) — all four combinations give x>y with no equality possible.

text: I. x² − 9x + 20 = 0  II. y² − 11y + 30 = 0. Find the relationship between x and y.
solution: Comparing every pair: (4,5)→x<y, (4,6)→x<y, (5,5)→x=y, (5,6)→x<y. x is never bigger than y, but can equal it — so the relationship is x ≤ y.

In a 200 m race, A gives B a start of 4 seconds and still beats him by 20 m. If A’s speed is 10 m/s, find B’s speed.
solution: A’s time for 200 m = 200 / 10 = 20 seconds.
B started 4 seconds earlier, so B has been running for 20 + 4 = 24 seconds when A finishes.
A beats B by 20 m, so in those 24 seconds B covered 200 − 20 = 180 m.

text: A and B run a 100 m race. A finishes in 10 seconds, and B finishes in 12.5 seconds (both at constant speed). By what distance does A beat B?
solution: At t = 10 seconds (when A finishes), B has covered 8 × 10 = 80 m.
A beats B by 100 − 80 = 20 m.

text: In a 100 m race, A gives B a start of 20 m. A’s speed is 10 m/s and B’s speed is 5 m/s. By how much time does A beat B?
solution: A runs the full 100 m: time = 100 / 10 = 10 seconds.
B only needs to cover 100 − 20 = 80 m: time = 80 / 5 = 16 seconds.
A beats B by 16 − 10 = 6 seconds.

text: In a 200 m race, A’s speed is 10 m/s and B’s speed is 8 m/s. What start should A give B so that the race ends in a dead heat (both finish together)?
solution: A’s time to finish 200 m = 200 / 10 = 20 seconds.
In that same 20 seconds, B covers 8 × 20 = 160 m.
For a dead heat, B’s required distance must also be 160 m, so the start = 200 − 160 = 40 m.

text: A and B run a 400 m race. A wins by 40 m or 10 seconds. Find A's speed.
solution: The "40 m or 10 seconds" phrasing means: the 40 m that B was still short of finishing is exactly what B would have covered in the 10 extra seconds. So B's speed = 40/10 = 4 m/s.
B's time to finish the full 400 m = 400/4 = 100 seconds.
A finishes 10 seconds before that: A's time = 100 − 10 = 90 seconds.

text: In a race, A can give B a start of 10 m in a 100 m race, and B can give C a start of 10 m in the same 100 m race. If A, B and C all ran a 100 m race together, by how much would A beat C?
solution: A gives B a 10 m start in 100 m, so while A covers 100 m, B covers 90 m: speed ratio B/A = 90/100 = 9/10.
Similarly, speed ratio C/B = 9/10.
Combine the ratios (don't just add the distances): speed ratio C/A = (9/10) × (9/10) = 81/100.
So while A covers 100 m, C covers 81 m. A beats C by 100 − 81 = 19 m (not 10 + 10 = 20 m).

text: In a 100 m race, A gives B a start of 5 seconds. If B's speed is 4 m/s, what is this equivalent to as a distance start?
solution: A time start of T seconds is equivalent to that runner covering T × speed metres before the other even begins.
Equivalent distance = 5 × 4 = 20 m.

Five friends — Aman, Bina, Chetan, Divya and Esha — visited a library on five different days of the same week, Monday to Friday, one person per day. Esha visited on Friday. Chetan visited immediately before Esha. Aman visited immediately before Chetan. Divya visited immediately after Bina. Bina did not visit on Tuesday. Who visited the library on Monday?
solution: Esha = Friday. Chetan (immediately before Esha) = Thursday. Aman (immediately before Chetan) = Wednesday.
Remaining days, Monday and Tuesday, go to Bina and Divya. Divya is immediately after Bina — among Monday/Tuesday, that only works as Bina = Monday, Divya = Tuesday.
So the full week is: Bina (Mon), Divya (Tue), Aman (Wed), Chetan (Thu), Esha (Fri).

text: Using the same puzzle and clues, how many people visited the library after Divya?
solution: Divya visited on Tuesday. After Tuesday come Wednesday (Aman), Thursday (Chetan), and Friday (Esha) — three people.

text: Using the same puzzle and clues, on which day did Divya visit the library?
solution: From the full arrangement, Divya visited on Tuesday.

text: Using the same puzzle and clues, who visited the library exactly two days after Bina?
solution: Bina visited on Monday. Two days after Monday is Wednesday, which is Aman’s day.

text: Using the same puzzle and clues, who visited the library immediately after Aman?
solution: From the full arrangement — Bina (Mon), Divya (Tue), Aman (Wed), Chetan (Thu), Esha (Fri) — the day immediately after Aman’s (Wednesday) is Thursday, which is Chetan.

text: Using the same puzzle and clues, how many people visited the library before Chetan?
solution: Chetan visited on Thursday. Before Thursday come Monday (Bina), Tuesday (Divya), and Wednesday (Aman) — three people.

text: Five people — A, B, C, D and E — visit a doctor in five different months (January, March, May, July, September) on five different dates (5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th), one person per month and one per date. A visits in May. C visits in the month immediately after A. E visits in September. B visits in January. E visits on the 5th. A visits on the 10th. The person who visits in January visits on the 20th. The person who visits in March visits on the 15th. Who visits in January?
solution: Months: A = May. C is immediately after May, so C = July. E = September. B = January (given directly). The only month left, March, goes to D.
Dates: E = 5th, A = 10th (given directly). The January person (B) visits on the 20th, so B = 20th. The March person (D) visits on the 15th, so D = 15th. The only date left, 25th, goes to C.
Full arrangement — A: May/10th, B: January/20th, C: July/25th, D: March/15th, E: September/5th.

Which of the following is NOT a component of scientific attitude? (A) Open-mindedness  (B) Curiosity  (C) Suspended judgement until sufficient evidence is available  (D) Accepting statements on the basis of authority without evidence
answer: (D) Accepting statements on the basis of authority without evidence. Scientific attitude includes curiosity, open-mindedness, objectivity, suspended judgement and respect for evidence. Accepting claims merely because of the authority of the person making them is the opposite of scientific attitude.

text: Which of the following is an ARCHAEOLOGICAL source of history? (A) Accounts written by foreign travellers  (B) Hymns of the Rigveda  (C) Old newspapers kept in an archive  (D) Pottery, tools, monuments and coins recovered from excavations
answer: (D) Pottery, tools, monuments and coins recovered from excavations. Archaeological sources are material remains obtained by excavation and survey: pottery, tools, buildings, coins, inscriptions. Travellers' accounts, Vedic texts and newspapers are literary or written sources.

text: After learning about evaporation, students are asked to explain why clothes dry faster on a windy day and why we feel cool after sweating. In the 5E model this activity belongs to the phase: (A) Engage  (B) Explore  (C) Explain  (D) Elaborate
answer: (D) Elaborate. The Elaborate phase asks students to apply and extend a newly learnt concept to new situations, deepening understanding and transfer. Explore is the initial hands-on investigation, before the concept is formalised.

text: A Class 7 student says, 'Plants get their food from the soil through their roots.' From a science teacher's point of view this is: (A) Fully correct  (B) Partially correct, since roots absorb ready-made food from the soil  (C) Correct only for crop plants  (D) A misconception; plants make their own food by photosynthesis, while soil supplies water and minerals
answer: (D) A misconception; plants make their own food by photosynthesis, while soil supplies water and minerals. Plants are autotrophs that synthesise food from carbon dioxide and water using light. The soil provides water and mineral nutrients, not food, so the belief must be addressed through activities on photosynthesis.

text: 'Design an experiment to find out which of three fabrics absorbs the most water.' This task mainly belongs to which level of the revised Bloom's taxonomy? (A) Remember  (B) Create  (C) Understand  (D) Apply
answer: (B) Create. Designing a new procedure requires students to plan, generate and produce an original investigation, which is the Create level. Apply would be using a given procedure in a familiar situation.

text: A history teacher asks, 'What changes did the introduction of railways bring about in the economy and society of colonial India?' The teacher is mainly developing the skill of: (A) Memorisation of dates  (B) Reading map symbols  (C) Reasoning about cause and effect  (D) Drawing historical monuments
answer: (C) Reasoning about cause and effect. Asking about consequences and changes brought by an event trains learners to link causes with effects, a core historical thinking skill, instead of recalling the year the railway opened.

text: The main purpose of organising a mock parliament in a Class 8 social science class is to: (A) Help students understand parliamentary procedures, debate and law-making through participation  (B) Provide entertainment on the annual day  (C) Make students memorise the numbers of constitutional Articles  (D) Elect the class monitor for the year
answer: (A) Help students understand parliamentary procedures, debate and law-making through participation. A mock parliament is a simulation in which students take roles of Speaker, ministers and opposition, so that abstract concepts such as question hour, bills and debate become concrete and understood from the inside.

text: Which statement correctly distinguishes 'social studies' from 'social sciences'? (A) The two terms mean exactly the same thing  (B) Social science is taught at the primary stage and social studies at the university stage  (C) Social studies deals only with history, while social sciences deal only with geography  (D) Social studies is the integrated school subject that draws on the specialised social science disciplines
answer: (D) Social studies is the integrated school subject that draws on the specialised social science disciplines. Social sciences are the academic disciplines (history, geography, political science, economics, sociology). Social studies is the school subject that integrates and simplifies their content for the purpose of citizenship education.

text: The primary purpose of organising a science exhibition or science fair in an upper primary school is to: (A) Rank schools on the basis of exhibits  (B) Develop creativity, innovation and scientific temper through self-made exhibits  (C) Help students memorise the textbook for the examination  (D) Award prizes to the best-dressed participants
answer: (B) Develop creativity, innovation and scientific temper through self-made exhibits. Science fairs give children a platform to apply science to real problems, build working models and communicate ideas, nurturing creativity, innovation and scientific attitude. Competition and prizes are incidental.

text: Which statement best captures the 'tentative' nature of scientific knowledge? (A) Scientific facts, once proved, can never be changed  (B) Scientific knowledge is open to revision in the light of new evidence  (C) Scientific knowledge depends on the opinion of famous scientists  (D) Scientific laws hold true only inside laboratories
answer: (B) Scientific knowledge is open to revision in the light of new evidence. Science is tentative because every conclusion remains open to modification when new evidence or better explanations appear. It is not fixed for ever, nor is it a matter of authority or opinion.

Improve the underlined part: "Each of the players were given a medal." (A) was given a medal (B) have been given a medal (C) were giving a medal (D) No improvement
solution: "Each of + plural noun" is treated as a singular subject, so the verb must be singular, not plural.
"were given" is plural; it should be "was given".

text: Improve the underlined part: "He does not know how to swim and nor can he dive." (A) and neither can he dive (B) and he also cannot dive (C) nor can he dive (D) No improvement
solution: "Nor" already carries the "and...not" meaning by itself — pairing it with "and" ("and nor") is redundant.
The correct form simply drops "and": "...nor can he dive".

solution: "Senior" is one of a small set of comparison words (senior, junior, prior, superior, inferior) that pair with "to", not "than".
It should read "senior to me".

text: Improve the underlined part: "She has been working here since five years." (A) for five years (B) from five years (C) since five years’ time (D) No improvement
solution: "Since" pairs with a specific POINT IN TIME (since 2020, since Monday); "for" pairs with a DURATION (for five years, for two hours).
"Five years" is a duration, not a point in time, so "since five years" is wrong — it should be "for five years".

solution: "If I had worked harder" is a past-hypothetical condition (third conditional) — describing something that did not actually happen.
The matching result clause for a third conditional is "would have + past participle", not plain "would + base verb" — so it should be "I would have passed the exam".

text: Find the next number in the series: 0, 1, 8, 27, 64, ?
solution: These are perfect cubes: 0³=0, 1³=1, 2³=8, 3³=27, 4³=64.
The next cube is 5³ = 125.

text: Find the missing number in the series: 1, 4, 2, 8, 3, 12, 4, ?
solution: This looks irregular as one sequence, so split it into odd-position and even-position terms.
Odd positions (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th): 1, 2, 3, 4 — increasing by 1 each time.
Even positions (2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th): 4, 8, 12, ? — increasing by 4 each time, so the next (8th) term is 16.

text: Find the next number in the series: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ?
solution: These are the prime numbers in order: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11.
The next prime number is 13.

text: Find the next number in the series: 3, 6, 4, 8, 6, 12, 10, ?
solution: A single alternating ±amount doesn't fit. Try a two-operation cycle instead: 3→6 is ×2, 6→4 is −2, 4→8 is ×2, 8→6 is −2, 6→12 is ×2, 12→10 is −2.
The cycle "×2, then −2" repeats consistently. The last operation shown was −2 (12→10), so the next is ×2.
Next term = 10 × 2 = 20.

text: Find the next number in the series: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ?
solution: Differences between consecutive terms: 5−2=3, 10−5=5, 17−10=7, 26−17=9.
The differences themselves are 3, 5, 7, 9 — increasing by 2 each time, so the next difference is 11.
Next term = 26 + 11 = 37. (This series is actually n² + 1 for n = 1, 2, 3, …)

text: Find the next number in the series: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, ?

text: In a survey of 100 people, 60 like tea and 50 like coffee. If 20 like both, how many like neither?
solution: Neither = Total − union = 100 − 90 = 10.

text: In a class of 60 students, 35 play cricket and 25 play football. If 10 students play both, how many play at least one of the two games?
solution: |Cricket ∪ Football| = 35 + 25 − 10 = 50.

text: In a group of 50 students, 30 study Math, 25 study Physics, and 15 study both. How many study only Math (not Physics)?
solution: Only Math = |Math| − |Math ∩ Physics| = 30 − 15 = 15.

text: In a class of 100 students: 50 play cricket, 40 play football, 30 play hockey. 15 play both cricket and football, 12 play both football and hockey, 10 play both cricket and hockey, and 5 play all three. How many play at least one of the three games?
Using the same data as above, how many students play none of the three games?
solution: None = Total − (at least one) = 100 − 88 = 12.

text: In a class of 80 students, 50 play cricket, 40 play football, and 20 play both. How many play exactly one of the two games?
solution: |Cricket ∪ Football| = 50 + 40 − 20 = 70.
Exactly one = union − both = 70 − 20 = 50.

3 pens and 2 pencils cost ₹78. 5 pens and 3 pencils cost ₹128. Find the cost of one pen and one pencil.
solution: Let a pen cost p and a pencil cost q: 3p + 2q = 78 … (1), and 5p + 3q = 128 … (2).
Scale to eliminate q: multiply (1) by 3 and (2) by 2: 9p + 6q = 234, and 10p + 6q = 256.
Subtract: p = 256 − 234 = 22. Substitute into (1): 3(22) + 2q = 78 → 66 + 2q = 78 → q = 6.

text: Five years ago, a father was three times as old as his son. Ten years from now, the father will be twice as old as the son. Find their present ages.
solution: Let the son’s present age = s and the father’s present age = f.
Five years ago: f − 5 = 3(s − 5), so f = 3s − 10.
Ten years from now: f + 10 = 2(s + 10), so f = 2s + 10.
Setting these equal: 3s − 10 = 2s + 10, so s = 20, and f = 2(20) + 10 = 50.

text: A number is 8 more than twice another number. If the sum of the two numbers is 50, find both numbers.
solution: Let the numbers be x and y, with x = 2y + 8.
Substituting into x + y = 50: (2y + 8) + y = 50, so 3y = 42, giving y = 14.

text: If 3 is added to both the numerator and denominator of a fraction, it becomes 3/4. If 1 is subtracted from both, it becomes 1/2. Find the original fraction.
solution: Let the fraction be x/y. (x+3)/(y+3) = 3/4 → 4x + 12 = 3y + 9 → 4x − 3y = −3 … (1).

text: The sum of two numbers is 45, and their difference is 11. Find the two numbers.
solution: Let the numbers be x and y: x + y = 45 and x − y = 11.
Adding the two equations: 2x = 56, so x = 28.
Substituting back: y = 45 − 28 = 17.

text: Three times a number, decreased by 7, equals twice the number increased by 9. Find the number.
solution: Let the number be x: 3x − 7 = 2x + 9.
Subtracting 2x from both sides: x − 7 = 9, so x = 16.

text: The sum of three consecutive integers is 72. Find the integers.
solution: Let the integers be x, x+1, x+2. Their sum: x + (x+1) + (x+2) = 72 → 3x + 3 = 72 → x = 23.
The integers are 23, 24, 25.

text: If 2 is added to both the numerator and denominator of a fraction, it becomes 1/2. If 1 is subtracted from both, it becomes 1/3. Find the original fraction.
answer: 4/10 (= 2/5). Solve y=2x+2 and y=3x-2 together to get x=4, y=10.

Statement: Should the use of private vehicles be restricted in city centres? Arguments: I. Yes, it would reduce traffic congestion and air pollution in densely populated areas. II. No, because some people might not like the restriction.
solution: I: Names specific, weighty, measurable consequences (congestion, pollution) directly tied to the proposal. Strong.
II: "Might not like it" is a vague personal reaction, not a weighty practical consequence. Weak.

text: Statement: Should schools introduce compulsory computer education from an early age? Arguments: I. Yes, early exposure to technology will better prepare students for a digital economy. II. No, it would require significant investment in infrastructure and teacher training that many schools cannot currently afford.
solution: I: A specific, weighty future benefit directly tied to the proposal. Strong.
II: A specific, weighty practical constraint directly tied to the proposal. Strong.

text: Statement: Should higher education be made completely free for all students? Arguments: I. Yes, it would make education accessible to economically weaker sections who currently cannot afford it. II. No, it would require the government to allocate significantly more funds, which could affect other essential public services.
solution: I: A specific, weighty benefit (access for those currently priced out) directly tied to the proposal. Strong.
II: A specific, weighty cost (funding tradeoffs against other services) directly tied to the proposal. Strong.

text: Statement: Should the government increase funding for space research? Arguments: I. Yes, because space is vast and interesting. II. No, because other countries also fund space research.
solution: I: "Interesting" isn’t a weighty justification for a funding priority — too vague. Weak.
II: Other countries’ funding choices don’t address whether this government should increase its own funding. Weak.

text: Statement: Should voting be made mandatory for all eligible citizens? Arguments: I. Yes, mandatory voting would increase voter turnout and ensure governments better reflect the will of the majority. II. No, people should be free to do whatever they want.
solution: I: Gives a specific, weighty reason — better representation through higher turnout. Strong.
II: A vague generalization about freedom that doesn’t engage with the specific tradeoffs of mandatory voting. Weak.

text: Statement: Should smoking be banned in all public places? Arguments: I. No, people have been smoking for centuries, so it should continue. II. Yes, passive smoking harms the health of non-smokers who have no choice in the matter.
solution: I: Tradition alone isn’t a reason to continue something with proven harms — this doesn’t engage with the actual issue. Weak.
II: A specific, weighty harm to non-consenting third parties — directly relevant to why a ban might be justified. Strong.

text: Statement: Should the city build a new stadium? Arguments: I. Yes, because sports are fun. II. No, because the old stadium already exists.

Statement: Should plastic bags be banned in retail stores? Arguments: I. Yes, plastic bags take hundreds of years to decompose and cause significant environmental harm. II. No, people like using plastic bags.

Statement: Should remote work be made a permanent option for all office employees? Arguments: I. Yes, it reduces commuting costs and time for employees. II. No, because some managers personally prefer seeing employees in the office.

Statement: Should companies be required to publicly disclose their environmental impact? Arguments: I. Yes, it would hold companies accountable and help consumers make informed choices. II. No, because the information might be misused.

Statement: Should employees be allowed to work from home permanently? Arguments: I. Yes, it reduces commuting time and increases work-life balance for employees. II. No, it can reduce spontaneous collaboration and weaken team cohesion over time.

Statement: "The school has decided to introduce a new online portal for submitting homework." Assumptions: I. Students have access to the internet and a device to use the portal. II. The current method of submitting homework has some drawback.
solution: I: An online portal is unusable without internet access and a device — the decision necessarily assumes students can get online. This is assumed.
II: Deciding to introduce a new system in place of an existing one assumes there’s some reason for the change — otherwise the decision wouldn’t make sense. This is also assumed.

text: Statement: "Keep off the grass." — a sign in a park. Assumptions: I. Some people might walk on the grass if not told not to. II. All visitors will obey the sign.
solution: I: A sign like this is put up precisely because there’s a real possibility people would otherwise walk on the grass. This is assumed.
II: Putting up a sign doesn’t require assuming 100% compliance — signs exist because not everyone obeys by default, with or without one.

text: Statement: "Admissions open for the new batch. Apply now!" — a coaching institute’s advertisement. Assumptions: I. Some people would be interested in applying. II. The new batch has already started.
solution: I: Advertisements only make sense if there’s a potential audience interested in what’s offered — without that, advertising would be pointless. This is assumed.
II: "Admissions open" suggests the batch has NOT started yet, if anything — this isn’t assumed, and even contradicts the statement.

text: Statement: "The company has decided to increase the price of its product from next month." Assumptions: I. Customers will stop buying the product due to the price increase. II. The company needs more profit to survive.
solution: I: Deciding to raise the price doesn’t assume customers will STOP buying — if anything, the opposite (that enough customers will keep buying) is what would make the decision sensible.
II: The statement doesn’t require this specific reason — there could be many other reasons (rising costs, higher demand) for a price increase, so this isn’t a necessary assumption.

text: Statement: "What time does the next train to Delhi leave?" — asked by a passenger at a railway inquiry counter. Assumptions: I. The person asked is likely to know the train timings. II. There is a next train to Delhi.
solution: I: Asking a specific question at an inquiry counter assumes that counter can plausibly answer it — that’s the whole reason to ask there.
II: Asking "what time does the NEXT train leave" presupposes there is one — otherwise the question wouldn’t make sense in that form.

text: Statement: "Buy our new smartphone, now available with a 2-year warranty." — an advertisement. Assumptions: I. Some customers value a longer warranty period. II. All customers will buy the smartphone because of the warranty.
solution: I: Highlighting the warranty as a selling point only makes sense if at least some buyers care about it. This is assumed.
II: An advertisement doesn’t assume every single customer will buy — that’s a far stronger claim than the statement needs.

text: Statement: "Mumbai is the financial capital of India." Assumptions: I. Some cities in India are not financial capitals. II. The speaker has visited Mumbai.

Statement: "Please maintain silence in the library." — a notice. Assumptions: I. Some people might talk if not asked not to. II. The library is always completely silent.

Statement: "All employees must submit their annual reports by Friday." Assumptions: I. Some employees have not yet submitted their reports. II. All employees are capable of completing their reports by Friday.

Statement: "The company will give a 10% bonus to employees who complete the project before the deadline." Assumptions: I. Some employees are capable of completing the project before the deadline. II. All employees will try to finish early because of the bonus.

Statement: "Either the manager or the supervisor will attend tomorrow’s meeting." Conclusions: I. If the manager does not attend, the supervisor will attend. II. Both the manager and the supervisor will attend.
solution: I: An "either...or" statement guarantees that if one option is ruled out, the other must happen — this follows directly.
II: The statement only guarantees at least one of them attends, not that both do — this goes beyond what was said.

text: Statement: "Out of 500 candidates who appeared for an exam, 320 were men and the rest were women." Conclusions: I. 180 women appeared for the exam. II. The exam was more difficult for the women candidates.
solution: I: 500 − 320 = 180 — a direct arithmetic restatement of the given numbers. This follows.
II: The statement gives no information about difficulty for either group; this is entirely unsupported.

text: Statement: "The number of applicants for the exam this year is 20% higher than last year." Conclusions: I. More people are interested in the exam this year than last year. II. The exam has become more difficult this year.
solution: I: Applying is a direct measure of interest, so more applicants directly means more interest — this follows.
II: The statement says nothing about difficulty; that’s an unstated guess about cause, not what was actually said.

text: Statement: "Ramesh is taller than Suresh, and Suresh is taller than Mohan." Conclusions: I. Ramesh is taller than Mohan. II. Mohan is the shortest among the three.
solution: I: Combining Ramesh > Suresh > Mohan directly gives Ramesh > Mohan.
II: Mohan sits at the bottom of the full established order among exactly these three, so Mohan is directly the shortest.

text: Statement: "All the 50 employees of the company attended the training session held last week." Conclusions: I. The company has 50 employees. II. The training session was held last week.
solution: I: Directly stated ("the 50 employees").
II: Directly stated ("held last week").

text: Statement: "Company X’s profits increased for three consecutive years, but fell sharply in the fourth year." Conclusions: I. The company faced some problem in the fourth year. II. The company’s management changed in the fourth year.
solution: I: A profit fall doesn’t directly prove any specific "problem" — it could result from many things (a one-time policy change, a deliberate price cut), so this isn’t a direct logical derivation.
II: The statement says nothing about management at all; this is entirely unsupported.

text: Statement: "Either the fan or the air conditioner in the room is malfunctioning." Conclusions: I. If the fan is not malfunctioning, the air conditioner is. II. Neither the fan nor the air conditioner is malfunctioning.

Statement: "City P has a population of 2 lakh, and City Q has a population of 3.5 lakh." Conclusions: I. City Q is more populated than City P. II. City P will have as large a population as City Q within 5 years.

Which of the following missiles was NOT developed under the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP)? (A) Agni  (B) BrahMos  (C) Nag  (D) Trishul
answer: (B) BrahMos. IGMDP, started in 1983 under A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, produced Prithvi, Agni, Trishul, Akash and Nag. BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile made by an Indo-Russian joint venture formed in 1998.

text: The final of the 1983 Cricket World Cup, which India won under Kapil Dev, was played at which ground? (A) The Oval  (B) Old Trafford  (C) Lord's  (D) Edgbaston
answer: (C) Lord's. India beat the West Indies by 43 runs at Lord's, London, on 25 June 1983. India's second World Cup win came in 2011 under M.S. Dhoni at the Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai, against Sri Lanka.

text: The Hirakud Dam, one of the longest dams in the world, is built on which river? (A) Mahanadi  (B) Godavari  (C) Krishna  (D) Narmada
answer: (A) Mahanadi. Hirakud Dam near Sambalpur in Odisha was completed in 1957 across the Mahanadi and is about 25.8 km long including dykes. Sardar Sarovar is on the Narmada and Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna.

text: Who was the first Indian citizen to travel into space? (A) Kalpana Chawla  (B) Ravish Malhotra  (C) Rakesh Sharma  (D) Sunita Williams
answer: (C) Rakesh Sharma. Wing Commander Rakesh Sharma flew aboard the Soviet Soyuz T-11 to the Salyut 7 station in April 1984. Ravish Malhotra was his backup; Kalpana Chawla and Sunita Williams flew as American astronauts.

text: National Science Day is celebrated on 28 February to mark which event? (A) Birth of C.V. Raman  (B) Award of the Nobel Prize to C.V. Raman  (C) Discovery of the Raman Effect  (D) Founding of CSIR
answer: (C) Discovery of the Raman Effect. C.V. Raman announced the discovery of the Raman Effect on 28 February 1928, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930. Raman was born on 7 November 1888.

text: Who wrote 'Jana Gana Mana', the National Anthem of India? (A) Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay  (B) Rabindranath Tagore  (C) Sarojini Naidu  (D) Subramania Bharati
answer: (B) Rabindranath Tagore. Tagore wrote it in Bengali; it was first sung on 27 December 1911 at the Calcutta session of the Congress and adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 24 January 1950. Bankim Chandra wrote the National Song, Vande Mataram.

text: Hargobind Khorana received the Nobel Prize in 1968 in which field? (A) Physiology or Medicine  (B) Physics  (C) Chemistry  (D) Economic Sciences
answer: (A) Physiology or Medicine. Khorana shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the genetic code. C.V. Raman (1930) and S. Chandrasekhar (1983) won in Physics and Venkatraman Ramakrishnan (2009) in Chemistry.

text: Which statement about the national sport of India is correct? (A) Hockey was officially declared the national sport in 1928  (B) Cricket is the officially declared national sport  (C) Kabaddi was declared the national sport in 1990  (D) No game has been officially declared as the national sport of India
answer: (D) No game has been officially declared as the national sport of India. In a 2012 RTI reply the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports clarified that no game has been declared the national sport. Hockey is popularly believed to be the national sport because of India's Olympic record, but there is no official declaration.

text: Which of the following organisation and headquarters pairs is correctly matched? (A) IMF - Washington DC  (B) UNESCO - Geneva  (C) WHO - Paris  (D) UNICEF - Vienna
answer: (A) IMF - Washington DC. The IMF and the World Bank, both born of the 1944 Bretton Woods conference, are headquartered in Washington DC. UNESCO is in Paris, WHO in Geneva and UNICEF in New York.

text: Mahatma Gandhi's autobiography 'The Story of My Experiments with Truth' was originally written in which language? (A) Hindi  (B) Gujarati  (C) English  (D) Marathi
answer: (B) Gujarati. Gandhi wrote it in Gujarati as Satya na Prayogo, serialised in Navajivan between 1925 and 1929, and Mahadev Desai translated it into English. Hind Swaraj (1909) was also written in Gujarati.

Statements: Some pens are books. All books are tables. Conclusions: I. Some pens are tables. II. Some tables are pens. Which conclusion(s) logically follow?
solution: Some pens are books means the "pens" circle and "books" circle overlap. All books are tables means the "books" circle sits entirely inside the "tables" circle.
The pens that overlap with books are therefore also inside tables — so some pens are tables. Conclusion I is forced.
"Some pens are tables" (just shown true) can always be flipped to "Some tables are pens" — this flip is always valid for "Some…are" statements. So Conclusion II follows too.

text: Statements: Some actors are singers. No singer is a dancer. Conclusions: I. No actor is a dancer. II. Some actors are dancers. Which conclusion(s) follow?
answer: Either Conclusion I or Conclusion II follows
solution: The actors who are also singers are definitely not dancers (since no singer is a dancer). But non-singer actors are completely unconstrained — they could all be dancers, or none of them could.
So Conclusion I ("No actor is a dancer") is too strong — it isn't forced. Conclusion II ("Some actors are dancers") also isn't forced — it's entirely possible that zero actors are dancers.

But these two conclusions are exact complements: either SOME actor is a dancer, or NO actor is — one of the two must be true. Since neither follows alone but one of them must hold, the answer is "Either I or II follows."

text: Statements: All cats are dogs. All dogs are cows. Conclusions: I. All cats are cows. II. All cows are cats. Which conclusion(s) logically follow?
solution: All cats are dogs means the "cats" circle sits entirely inside the "dogs" circle. All dogs are cows means the "dogs" circle sits entirely inside the "cows" circle.
So the "cats" circle is entirely inside the "cows" circle too — Conclusion I is forced in every possible arrangement.
Conclusion II is not forced — the "cows" circle could easily be much bigger, containing cows that are neither dogs nor cats. It does not follow.

text: Statements: No apples are oranges. Some oranges are fruits. Conclusions: I. Some fruits are not apples. II. No apples are fruits. Which conclusion(s) logically follow?
solution: No apples are oranges means the "apples" circle and "oranges" circle do not overlap at all.

Some oranges are fruits means part of the "oranges" circle overlaps with the "fruits" circle — and that overlapping part, being entirely within oranges, cannot contain any apples (since apples and oranges never overlap).
So those particular fruits (the ones that are oranges) are definitely not apples — "Some fruits are not apples" is forced. Conclusion I follows.

"No apples are fruits" is not forced — apples could still overlap with fruits through some path that has nothing to do with oranges; nothing in the statements rules that out. Conclusion II does not follow.

text: Statements: All mangoes are fruits. All fruits are healthy foods. Some healthy foods are expensive. Conclusion: Some mangoes are expensive. Does it follow?
solution: Combining the first two statements: all mangoes are healthy foods (mangoes sit entirely inside healthy foods).
But "some healthy foods are expensive" only guarantees an overlap SOMEWHERE inside healthy foods — that overlap might sit entirely outside the mango subset.
So "Some mangoes are expensive" is not forced — it does not follow.

text: Statements: All mangoes are fruits. All fruits are healthy foods. All healthy foods are nutritious. Conclusion: All mangoes are nutritious. Does it follow?
solution: This chain is "All...All...All" throughout, so transitivity carries all the way through: mangoes ⊆ fruits ⊆ healthy foods ⊆ nutritious things.
So all mangoes are nutritious — the conclusion follows.

text: Statements: All books are pens. No pen is a pencil. Conclusions: I. No book is a pencil. II. Some pens are books. Which conclusion(s) logically follow?
solution: All books are pens means the "books" circle sits entirely inside the "pens" circle. No pen is a pencil means the "pens" circle and "pencils" circle do not overlap at all.

Since the "books" circle is entirely inside the "pens" circle, and the "pens" circle never touches the "pencils" circle, the "books" circle can’t touch the "pencils" circle either — "No book is a pencil" is forced. Conclusion I follows.
"All books are pens" guarantees every book is a pen, and since books exist, at least some pens are books — "Some pens are books" is forced. Conclusion II follows.

text: Choose the antonym of "BENEVOLENT": (A) Generous (B) Malevolent (C) Wealthy (D) Famous
solution: "Benevolent" (from "bene-" = good) means kind and well-meaning.
"Malevolent" (from "mal-" = bad) means wishing harm to others — the direct opposite.
"Generous" (A) is close in meaning to benevolent, not its opposite.

text: Choose the antonym of "GENEROUS": (A) Kind (B) Wealthy (C) Stingy (D) Friendly
solution: "Generous" means willing to give freely. Its opposite is being unwilling to give — "stingy".
"Kind" and "Friendly" (A, D) are actually close in meaning to generous, not its opposite. "Wealthy" (B) describes having money, which is unrelated to willingness to share it.

Two trains, 150 m and 100 m long, run on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 45 km/hr and 36 km/hr respectively. In how much time will they completely cross each other?
solution: Moving in opposite directions, relative speed = sum of speeds = 45 + 36 = 81 km/hr.
Convert to m/s: 81 × 5/18 = 22.5 m/s.
To completely cross each other, together they must cover a distance equal to the sum of both train lengths: 150 + 100 = 250 m.
Time = Distance / Speed = 250 / 22.5 = 100/9 ≈ 11.1 seconds.

text: Convert a speed of 72 km/hr into metres per second.

text: A man travels from town A to town B at 40 km/hr, and returns from B to A by the same road at 60 km/hr. Find his average speed for the entire journey.
solution: The distance each way is the same, so the simple average (40 + 60)/2 = 50 km/hr is WRONG here — that shortcut only works when the TIME spent at each speed is equal, not the distance.
For two equal distances covered at speeds a and b, average speed = 2ab / (a + b).

text: Towns A and B are 300 km apart. A car starts from A towards B at 50 km/hr at the same time as another car starts from B towards A at 70 km/hr. After how long do they meet, and how far from A?
answer: They meet after 2.5 hours, 125 km from A
solution: Moving toward each other, combined speed = 50 + 70 = 120 km/hr.
Time to meet = Distance / combined speed = 300 / 120 = 2.5 hours.
Distance from A = speed from A × time = 50 × 2.5 = 125 km.

text: A train's speed excluding stoppages is 60 km/hr, and its average speed including stoppages is 45 km/hr. Find the number of minutes per hour the train is stopped.
solution: Fraction of each hour "lost" to stoppages = 1 − (effective speed / running speed) = 1 − 45/60 = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25.
Stoppage time per hour = 0.25 × 60 minutes
= 15 minutes

text: A man travels 60 km at 30 km/hr, and then a further 90 km at 45 km/hr. Find his average speed for the whole journey.
solution: The two distances (60 km and 90 km) are not equal, so the 2ab/(a + b) shortcut does not apply here — use total distance / total time instead.
Time for the first part = 60/30 = 2 hours. Time for the second part = 90/45 = 2 hours.
Total distance = 60 + 90 = 150 km. Total time = 2 + 2 = 4 hours.
Average speed = 150 / 4 = 37.5 km/hr.

text: A car travels at a constant speed of 60 km/hr. How long will it take to cover 180 km?
solution: Time = Distance / Speed
= 3 hours

text: Two trains 120 m and 180 m long move in the same direction at 72 km/hr and 54 km/hr. Find the time the faster train takes to completely pass the slower one.
answer: 60 seconds. Relative speed = 72−54 = 18 km/hr = 5 m/s; distance = 120+180 = 300 m; time = 300/5.

text: A can complete a work in 10 days and B can complete the same work in 15 days. If they work together, in how many days will they finish it?
solution: A’s rate = 1/10, B’s rate = 1/15 per day.
Combined rate = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6 of the work per day.
Time to finish together = 1 ÷ (1/6) = 6 days.

text: 12 men can build a wall in 15 days. How many men, working at the same rate, are needed to build it in 10 days?
solution: For the same total work, Men × Days stays constant: 12 × 15 = 180.
For 10 days: Men = 180 / 10
= 18 men

text: A and B together can complete a work in 12 days. A alone can complete it in 20 days. In how many days can B alone complete the work?
solution: Combined rate (A + B) = 1/12. A’s rate = 1/20.
B’s time alone = 1 ÷ (1/30) = 30 days.

text: A can finish a work in 10 days and B in 15 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. In how many days will the work finish?
solution: A's rate = 1/10, B's rate = 1/15. In each 2-day cycle (one day A, one day B), work done = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6.
After 6 cycles (12 days), work done = 6 × 1/6 = 1 — exactly the whole job, with no leftover day to analyse.
So the work finishes in exactly 12 days.

text: A can complete a piece of work in 12 days. What fraction of the work does he complete in 4 days?
solution: A’s rate = 1/12 of the work per day.
Work done in 4 days = 4 × (1/12) = 4/12

text: A can do a piece of work in 20 days. B is 25% more efficient than A. Find the number of days B alone takes to complete the same work.
solution: "25% more efficient" means B’s work rate is 1.25 times A’s rate.
Since time is inversely proportional to rate, B’s time = A’s time ÷ 1.25 = 20 ÷ 1.25
= 16 days

text: A and B together can complete a work in 12 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves, and B alone completes the remaining work in 16 more days. In how many days could B alone have completed the entire work?
solution: Combined rate = 1/12. Work done in the first 4 days = 4 × 1/12 = 1/3.
Remaining work = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3, and B alone finishes this in 16 days, so B's rate = (2/3) / 16 = 1/24.
B alone would take 1 ÷ (1/24) = 24 days for the entire work.

text: A can finish a work in 8 days and B in 12 days. They work on alternate days, starting with A. In how many days will the work be completed?
answer: 9.5 days. 4 full cycles (8 days) complete 5/6 of the work; day 9 (A) adds 1/8, leaving 1/24; B finishes that 1/24 in half a day at B's rate of 1/12 per day.

text: If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is acute, find cos θ.

text: Uttar Pradesh shares its international boundary with which country? (A) Bhutan  (B) China  (C) Nepal  (D) Bangladesh
answer: (C) Nepal. UP shares a long international border with Nepal in the north through seven districts from Pilibhit to Maharajganj. It has no border with China, Bhutan or Bangladesh.

text: Meerut is a major Indian centre for the manufacture of: (A) Sports goods and scissors  (B) Silk sarees  (C) Brass utensils  (D) Chikan embroidery
answer: (A) Sports goods and scissors. Meerut, with Jalandhar, dominates India's sports goods industry, especially cricket equipment, and is also known for scissors. Chikankari belongs to Lucknow and brass to Moradabad.

text: At which site in Uttar Pradesh did Gautama Buddha deliver his first sermon, the Dharmachakra Pravartana? (A) Kushinagar  (B) Sarnath  (C) Shravasti  (D) Kaushambi
answer: (B) Sarnath. Buddha gave his first sermon at the Deer Park in Sarnath near Varanasi. Kushinagar is where he attained Mahaparinirvana, and Shravasti is where he spent many rainy seasons.

text: Okhla Bird Sanctuary, a wetland on the Yamuna popular with migratory birds, is located in which district? (A) Ghaziabad  (B) Bulandshahr  (C) Meerut  (D) Gautam Buddh Nagar
answer: (D) Gautam Buddh Nagar. Okhla Bird Sanctuary lies at the Okhla barrage on the Yamuna in Gautam Buddh Nagar (Noida), on the Delhi-UP border.

text: The National Chambal Sanctuary, spread across Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, is principally known for the conservation of: (A) Swamp deer and tiger  (B) Gharial and Gangetic dolphin  (C) Great Indian bustard  (D) One-horned rhinoceros
answer: (B) Gharial and Gangetic dolphin. The Chambal sanctuary protects the critically endangered gharial, the Gangetic dolphin and red-crowned roof turtles in the clean waters of the Chambal.

text: The Chambal river joins the Yamuna in which district of Uttar Pradesh? (A) Agra  (B) Etawah  (C) Jalaun  (D) Hamirpur
answer: (B) Etawah. The Chambal meets the Yamuna near Bhareh in Etawah district. The Betwa joins the Yamuna at Hamirpur and the Ken joins it in Banda district.

text: Who founded the autonomous Nawabi of Awadh in 1722? (A) Shuja-ud-Daula  (B) Asaf-ud-Daula  (C) Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk  (D) Wajid Ali Shah

text: Using the same data (A in 10 days, B in 15 days, total wage ₹3000), find B’s share.

text: A and B together can complete a work in 12 days. A alone can do it in 20 days. Working together, they earn ₹2400. Find B’s share.
solution: Combined rate = 1/12, A’s rate = 1/20. B’s rate = 1/12 − 1/20. Using a common denominator of 60: 5/60 − 3/60 = 2/60.
Ratio A : B = 3/60 : 2/60 = 3 : 2, total 5 parts. B’s share = 2/5 × ₹2400 = ₹960.

text: A can complete a work in 10 days and B in 15 days. A works on the job for 4 days and B works for 9 days (not necessarily at the same time), and together they just complete the work. If the total wage is ₹2000, find each person's share based on actual work done.
solution: A's actual work = 4 × (1/10) = 2/5. B's actual work = 9 × (1/15) = 3/5. Check: 2/5 + 3/5 = 1, the whole job — consistent.
Since the days worked are unequal, split by actual work done, not by the bare rates: ratio = 2/5 : 3/5 = 2 : 3.

text: A, B and C together can complete a work in 6 days. A alone can do it in 12 days, and B alone in 18 days. Working together, they earn ₹1800. Find C’s share.
solution: Combined rate = 1/6. A’s rate = 1/12, B’s rate = 1/18.
C’s rate = 1/6 − 1/12 − 1/18. Using a common denominator of 36: 6/36 − 3/36 − 2/36 = 1/36.

text: A and B together can complete a work in 12 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves and B completes the remaining work alone in 16 more days. If the total wage for the whole job is ₹4,800, find each person's share based on actual work done.
solution: Combined rate = 1/12. Work done in the first 4 days = 4/12 = 1/3, so the remaining work = 2/3.
B alone finishes 2/3 in 16 days, so B's rate = (2/3)/16 = 1/24. Then A's rate = 1/12 − 1/24 = 1/24 (the same as B's, in this case).

During the first 4 days, A contributed 4 × 1/24 = 1/6, and B also contributed 4 × 1/24 = 1/6. B then contributed a further 2/3 alone. B's total = 1/6 + 2/3 = 5/6. A's total = 1/6. (Check: 1/6 + 5/6 = 1.)

text: A can complete a work in 10 days and B can complete the same work in 15 days. They work together and complete it, earning a total of ₹3000. Find A’s share.

text: Which of the following regions has an equatorial (tropical rainforest) climate? (A) Sahara  (B) Siberia  (C) Amazon basin  (D) Arabian peninsula
answer: (C) Amazon basin. The Amazon basin, Congo basin, Malaysia and Indonesia have hot, wet equatorial climate throughout the year with no distinct seasons.

text: An ox-bow lake is formed by: (A) a glacier  (B) a river meander  (C) the wind  (D) groundwater
answer: (B) a river meander. In the old stage, on the floodplain, a river cuts across the neck of a meander and the abandoned loop becomes an ox-bow lake.

text: Winds are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere because of the: (A) Coriolis force  (B) Gravitational force  (C) Centripetal force  (D) Pressure gradient force
answer: (A) Coriolis force. The Coriolis force, arising from the Earth's rotation, deflects winds (Ferrel's law); it is zero at the Equator and maximum at the poles.

text: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean Sea with the: (A) Persian Gulf  (B) Red Sea  (C) Black Sea  (D) Arabian Sea

text: The Earth is nearest to the Sun (perihelion) around: (A) 4 July  (B) 21 June  (C) 3 January  (D) 22 December
